6.4 Choosing K — The Elbow Method AN306 AN300

K is the single most important hyperparameter in K-Means and must be specified before fitting. You don't always know the right K. The elbow method is the standard approach for selecting K based on inertia.

How the Elbow Method Works

The idea is simple: fit K-Means for K = 1, 2, 3, …, up to some maximum. Plot inertia (total within-cluster sum of squares) on the y-axis against K on the x-axis. As K increases, inertia always decreases — adding more clusters can always reduce within-cluster variation. But the rate of decrease slows.

The "elbow" is the point where the inertia curve bends sharply — the point of diminishing returns. Before the elbow, adding one more cluster reduces inertia a lot. After the elbow, adding more clusters gives smaller and smaller improvements. The elbow point is the suggested optimal K.

💡 Reading the Elbow: A Concrete Example

Suppose you get these inertia values as K increases:

KInertiaDrop from previous K
11,200—
2650−550 (big drop!)
3340−310 (big drop!)
4310−30 (small)
5295−15 (tiny)

The elbow is at K=3. Going from K=3 to K=4 only saves 30 units of inertia — not worth the added complexity. After K=3 you're just splitting natural groups into smaller pieces for diminishing gains.

Implementation

# ── Compute inertia for K = 1 to 12 ─────────────────────────────
inertias = []
K_range = range(1, 13)

for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
    km.fit(X_scaled)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)

# ── Plot the Elbow Curve ─────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.plot(K_range, inertias, 'o-', color='steelblue', lw=2, ms=8)
ax.axvline(x=3, color='tomato', linestyle='--', lw=1.5, label='Elbow at K=3')
ax.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (K)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('Inertia (Within-Cluster SSE)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Elbow Method for Optimal K', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13))
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_02_elbow.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

print("K → Inertia:")
for k, sse in zip(K_range, inertias):
    drop = '' if k == 1 else f'  Δ = {inertias[k-2] - sse:,.1f}'
    print(f"  K={k}: {sse:>10,.1f}{drop}")
💡 Reading the Elbow — Actual Inertia Numbers

Here's what a real inertia table might look like for the job market dataset:

KInertiaDrop from K−1Drop slowing?
11,450——
2620−830No — huge drop
3285−335No — still big
4230−55Yes — small drop ← elbow here
5195−35Yes — diminishing
6170−25Yes — diminishing

The elbow is at K=3 → K=4: inertia dropped by 830, then 335, then only 55. That sudden slowdown (from −335 to −55) is the bend in the curve. The model already captured most of the natural structure at K=3; adding a 4th cluster buys very little. K=3 is the answer.

In code, print(f"K={k}: {sse:>10,.1f} Δ={drop:,.1f}") gives you this table instantly — read the Δ column to spot where the drops plateau.

⚠ The Elbow Is Sometimes Ambiguous
Real-world data often has a gradual curve with no sharp elbow. When that happens, use the elbow method to narrow the range (e.g., "K is probably between 3 and 6"), then use silhouette scores (Module 6.5) to choose the best within that range. Never rely on just one method.

Computing Percentage of Variance Explained

# An alternative view: % of variance explained as K increases
total_sse = KMeans(n_clusters=1, random_state=42).fit(X_scaled).inertia_
var_explained = [(1 - sse/total_sse)*100 for sse in inertias]

for k, pct in zip(K_range, var_explained):
    print(f"K={k}: {pct:.1f}% variance explained")

6.5 Silhouette Analysis AN306

The silhouette score measures how well-separated clusters are by considering both the within-cluster cohesion and the between-cluster separation for each point. It is a richer evaluation than inertia alone.

The Silhouette Score Formula

For each point i: a(i) = mean distance from point i to all other points in its cluster (cohesion) b(i) = mean distance from point i to all points in the NEAREST other cluster (separation) Silhouette score for point i: s(i) = (b(i) − a(i)) / max(a(i), b(i)) Overall silhouette score = mean of s(i) over all points
💡 Silhouette by Hand

Say point P is in Cluster A. The 3 other points in its cluster are at distances 1.0, 1.2, and 0.8 from P. The nearest other cluster (B) has points at distances 2.5, 3.0, and 2.8 from P.

a(P) = average distance within cluster = (1.0 + 1.2 + 0.8) / 3 = 1.0
b(P) = average distance to nearest other cluster = (2.5 + 3.0 + 2.8) / 3 = 2.77

s(P) = (2.77 − 1.0) / max(1.0, 2.77) = 1.77 / 2.77 = 0.64 — a well-placed point (close to 1).

If P were on a cluster boundary where a(P) ≈ b(P) ≈ 2.0, then s(P) ≈ 0 — that point is ambiguous. If a(P) = 3.0 and b(P) = 1.0, s(P) is negative — the point was assigned to the wrong cluster.

Interpreting Silhouette Values

RangeInterpretation
s(i) close to +1Point is well-matched to its own cluster, far from neighboring clusters — excellent
s(i) close to 0Point is on or near the boundary between two clusters — ambiguous
s(i) close to −1Point is probably assigned to the wrong cluster — poor

Using Silhouette to Choose K

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# ── Compute silhouette for K = 2 to 12 ──────────────────────────
# (K=1 is undefined — no "other cluster" to compare)
silhouette_scores = []
K_range_sil = range(2, 13)

for k in K_range_sil:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    score = silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels)
    silhouette_scores.append(score)
    print(f"K={k}: silhouette = {score:.4f}")

# ── Plot Silhouette by K ─────────────────────────────────────────
best_k_sil = K_range_sil[np.argmax(silhouette_scores)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.plot(K_range_sil, silhouette_scores, 'o-', color='#56d9b0', lw=2, ms=8)
ax.axvline(x=best_k_sil, color='tomato', linestyle='--', lw=1.5,
           label=f'Best K={best_k_sil} (silhouette={max(silhouette_scores):.3f})')
ax.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (K)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('Silhouette Score', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Silhouette Analysis for Optimal K', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xticks(range(2, 13))
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_03_silhouette.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Silhouette Plot (Per-Point)

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_samples

# ── Detailed silhouette plot for K=3 ────────────────────────────
k_best = 3
km_best = KMeans(n_clusters=k_best, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels_best = km_best.fit_predict(X_scaled)

sil_vals  = silhouette_samples(X_scaled, labels_best)
sil_avg   = silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels_best)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
y_lower = 10
colors = ['#7c8ff5', '#56d9b0', '#f59e45']

for k in range(k_best):
    sil_k = np.sort(sil_vals[labels_best == k])
    size_k = sil_k.shape[0]
    y_upper = y_lower + size_k

    ax.fill_betweenx(np.arange(y_lower, y_upper), 0, sil_k,
                     alpha=0.7, color=colors[k], label=f'Cluster {k}')
    ax.text(-0.05, y_lower + 0.5*size_k, str(k), fontsize=10, color=colors[k], fontweight='bold')
    y_lower = y_upper + 10

ax.axvline(x=sil_avg, color='red', linestyle='--', lw=1.5, label=f'Mean = {sil_avg:.3f}')
ax.set_xlabel('Silhouette Coefficient', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title(f'Silhouette Plot — K={k_best}', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_04_silhouette_detail.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

6.6 K-Means++ Initialization AN306

Standard K-Means picks initial centroids completely at random, which can lead to bad starting configurations where two centroids are initialized close together and converge to a suboptimal solution. K-Means++ fixes this with a smarter initialization strategy.

K-Means++ Algorithm

  1. Choose the first centroid uniformly at random from the data points.
  2. For each remaining data point xᵢ, compute D(xᵢ) = the squared distance from xᵢ to the nearest centroid already chosen.
  3. Choose the next centroid with probability proportional to D(xᵢ)² — points that are farther from existing centroids have a higher probability of being selected.
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until K centroids have been chosen.
  5. Proceed with the standard K-Means assignment and update steps.

Why It Works

By spreading initial centroids far apart, K-Means++ reduces the chance that two centroids start near the same group and "compete" for the same cluster. This leads to:

  • Fewer iterations to convergence
  • Lower final inertia (better solutions)
  • More consistent results across runs (less variance between n_init attempts)
💡 K-Means++ Selection in Practice

Say K=2 and you have 4 data points: A=(0,0), B=(1,0), C=(9,0), D=(10,0). Two obvious clusters: {A,B} on the left and {C,D} on the right.

Step 1: Pick the first centroid randomly — say it lands on A=(0,0).

Step 2: Compute D²(xᵢ) for each remaining point (squared distance to nearest centroid A):

D²(B) = (1−0)² = 1  |  D²(C) = (9−0)² = 81  |  D²(D) = (10−0)² = 100

Step 3: Total = 1+81+100 = 182. Selection probabilities:
B → 1/182 ≈ 0.5%  |  C → 81/182 ≈ 44.5%  |  D → 100/182 ≈ 55%

C or D is overwhelmingly likely to become the second centroid — which is exactly right, since we want one centroid per natural group. Random init could have picked B, putting both centroids on the same side.

✓ Always Use K-Means++
In scikit-learn, K-Means++ is the default: init='k-means++'. There is almost never a reason to use init='random'. The computational cost of K-Means++ initialization is negligible, and the quality improvement is consistent. 
# Demonstration: random init vs K-Means++ init (10 runs each)
print("Comparing inertia: random vs k-means++ init (K=3, 10 trials each)")
print(f"{'Run':>4}  {'Random':>12}  {'K-Means++':>12}")

for trial in range(1, 11):
    km_rand = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init='random',    n_init=1, random_state=trial*7)
    km_pp   = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init='k-means++', n_init=1, random_state=trial*7)
    km_rand.fit(X_scaled)
    km_pp.fit(X_scaled)
    print(f"{trial:>4}  {km_rand.inertia_:>12.2f}  {km_pp.inertia_:>12.2f}")

6.7 Feature Scaling for Clustering AN306 Docx

Because K-Means uses Euclidean distance, features with larger numerical ranges dominate the distance calculation. A feature ranging 0–100,000 will contribute 10,000× more to distance than a feature ranging 0–10 — even if both are equally important for grouping observations. Feature scaling ensures every feature contributes proportionally.

Standardization (Z-score Scaling)

z = (x − μ) / σ

Subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation (σ). The result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. This is StandardScaler in scikit-learn.

⚠ Source Error — Built In Article
One of the linked readings stated "standardization divides by variance." This is WRONG. Standardization divides by the standard deviation (σ), not the variance (σ²). The formula is z = (x − μ) / σ. Dividing by variance would produce values in units of σ⁻¹, not the standard z-score scale. Always use σ in the denominator.

Min-Max Normalization

x_norm = (x − x_min) / (x_max − x_min)

Rescales values to the [0, 1] range. Use MinMaxScaler when you need bounded output or when you know the range is meaningful. Sensitive to outliers — one extreme outlier compresses all other values toward the middle.

Standardization vs. Normalization for Clustering

MethodRangeOutlier sensitivityWhen to use for clustering
StandardScaler (z-score)Unbounded (~−3 to +3)ModerateDefault choice for K-Means — most robust
MinMaxScaler[0, 1]High (outliers compress the rest)When all features are truly bounded with no outliers
RobustScalerUnboundedLow (uses median + IQR)When data has many outliers you want to keep
 
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler

# Standard (default for clustering)
X_std   = StandardScaler().fit_transform(data[['salary','years_exp','skill_score']])

# Min-Max
X_minmax = MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(data[['salary','years_exp','skill_score']])

# Robust
X_robust = RobustScaler().fit_transform(data[['salary','years_exp','skill_score']])

# Compare column statistics after scaling
print("After StandardScaler:  mean={:.4f}  std={:.4f}".format(
    X_std.mean(), X_std.std()))
print("After MinMaxScaler:    min={:.4f}   max={:.4f}".format(
    X_minmax.min(), X_minmax.max()))

# IMPORTANT: fit_transform on training/all data only
# If you later add new observations and want to assign them to clusters,
# use scaler.transform(new_data) — do NOT refit the scaler on new data
# (this is the same train-only fit rule as in Part 3)

6.8 Hierarchical Clustering AN306 AN300

Hierarchical clustering is an entirely different approach to grouping. Instead of starting with K clusters and iterating, it builds a tree of nested clusters — a dendrogram — that you can "cut" at any level to produce any number of clusters K without refitting.

Agglomerative vs. Divisive

There are two directions:

  • Agglomerative (bottom-up): Start with every observation as its own cluster (n clusters), then iteratively merge the two most similar clusters until one cluster remains. This is by far the most common approach and what AN306 uses.
  • Divisive (top-down): Start with all observations in one cluster, then split recursively. Rarely used in practice.

Linkage Criteria

At each step of agglomerative clustering, you need to define "distance between two clusters" (not just between two points). This is the linkage criterion:

LinkageDistance MeasureBehaviorBest For
WardIncrease in within-cluster variance when mergingMinimizes total within-cluster SSE; tends to produce compact, equal-size clustersDefault for most applications; best for compact clusters
CompleteMaximum distance between any two points across the two clustersConservative; prevents chaining; compact clustersWhen outliers need to be contained
AverageMean distance between all pairs of points across the two clustersCompromise between single and completeGeneral purpose
SingleMinimum distance between any two points across the two clusters"Chaining" tendency — one large elongated cluster formsDetecting elongated clusters; usually not ideal
💡 Plain-English Example: Why Ward Linkage Wins

Imagine you have two tight groups of points — Group A (tightly packed) and Group B (tightly packed, far from A) — plus a bridge point C halfway between them.

Single linkage measures the closest pair across clusters. C is fairly close to both A and B, so single linkage merges all three into one giant cluster too early. Result: one big blob instead of two clean groups — the "chaining" problem.

Ward linkage asks: "If I merge these two clusters, how much does the total within-cluster variance jump?" Merging A+B would cause a huge variance jump (they're far apart). Merging small nearby clusters costs little variance. Ward will naturally keep A and B separate until the very last steps, giving you the clearest structure. This is why Ward is the default for most clustering tasks.

Implementation

from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage

# ── Fit agglomerative clustering ──────────────────────────────────
# Ward linkage minimizes within-cluster variance at each step
agg = AgglomerativeClustering(
    n_clusters=3,
    linkage='ward'     # 'ward', 'complete', 'average', 'single'
)
agg_labels = agg.fit_predict(X_scaled)

data['cluster_agg'] = agg_labels
print("Agglomerative cluster sizes:")
print(data['cluster_agg'].value_counts().sort_index())

# ── Silhouette score for agglomerative result ─────────────────────
agg_sil = silhouette_score(X_scaled, agg_labels)
print(f"Silhouette score (Ward, K=3): {agg_sil:.4f}")

6.9 Dendrograms AN306

A dendrogram visualizes the entire merge history of hierarchical clustering. It is the definitive output of agglomerative clustering — it shows which observations were merged, in what order, and at what distance (height). By drawing a horizontal cutline at a chosen height, you can read off any number of clusters K.

Reading a Dendrogram

  • The x-axis shows individual observations (or small groups already merged)
  • The y-axis shows the linkage distance (Ward = variance increase; higher = more dissimilar)
  • Each horizontal bar represents a merge of two groups at the labeled height
  • A vertical cutline at height h gives you as many clusters as the line crosses branches
  • Long vertical bars before a cutline indicate well-separated natural clusters
💡 Plain-English Example: Cutting a Dendrogram

Say you have 5 job candidates: Alice, Bob, Charlie, Dana, Eve. After running hierarchical clustering, the merge history looks like this (read bottom to top):

Height 0.5: Alice + Bob merge (they're very similar — both junior Python devs)
Height 0.8: Charlie + Dana merge (both mid-level data engineers)
Height 1.2: (Alice+Bob) + Eve merge (Eve is also junior-ish)
Height 3.1: (Alice+Bob+Eve) + (Charlie+Dana) merge (now we're connecting juniors to mid-levels)

Draw a horizontal line at height 2.0. It crosses 2 vertical branches — so you get 2 clusters: {Alice, Bob, Eve} and {Charlie, Dana}.

Draw it at height 1.0. It crosses 3 branches — 3 clusters: {Alice, Bob}, {Eve}, {Charlie, Dana}.

The long gap between height 1.2 and 3.1 is the signal — that's where natural structure lives. Place your cut in the middle of the longest vertical bar you can find.

# ── Compute full linkage matrix ───────────────────────────────────
# scipy's linkage function does the full hierarchical computation
# subsample to 100 points for legible dendrogram display
idx = np.random.choice(len(X_scaled), size=100, replace=False)
X_sub = X_scaled[idx]

Z = linkage(X_sub, method='ward')

# ── Plot dendrogram ───────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 6))
dendrogram(
    Z,
    ax=ax,
    truncate_mode='lastp',  # show only the last p merges
    p=20,                   # show last 20 merges for readability
    color_threshold=3.5,    # color branches below this height
    leaf_rotation=90,
    leaf_font_size=9
)
ax.set_title('Dendrogram — Ward Linkage (subsample n=100)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel('Observation Index')
ax.set_ylabel('Ward Linkage Distance (Δ Within-Cluster Variance)')
ax.axhline(y=3.5, color='tomato', linestyle='--', lw=1.5, label='Cut at 3.5 → 3 clusters')
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_05_dendrogram.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Choosing K from the Dendrogram

# Find the ideal cut: look for the longest vertical bar you can cut
# The n largest gaps between merge heights suggest natural K values
merge_heights = Z[:, 2]  # the merge distances (column 2 of Z)
height_diffs  = np.diff(merge_heights)

# Top-5 largest jumps in merge height (working from the last merges)
largest_gaps = np.argsort(height_diffs)[-5:][::-1]
print("Largest gaps in merge height (suggests natural K values):")
for idx in largest_gaps:
    n_clusters = len(merge_heights) - idx  # clusters if cut after this merge
    print(f"  Gap of {height_diffs[idx]:.3f} at merge {idx} → cut here = ~{n_clusters} clusters")

6.10 DBSCAN AN306

DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) takes a completely different approach. Instead of assigning every point to a cluster, it defines clusters as dense regions separated by sparse regions — and labels any point in a sparse region as an outlier (noise), cluster label = −1.

DBSCAN Core Concepts

DBSCAN has two parameters: epsilon (ε) and min_samples.

  • Epsilon (ε): The neighborhood radius. A point's ε-neighborhood is the set of all points within distance ε of it.
  • min_samples: The minimum number of points (including the point itself) that must be in its ε-neighborhood for it to be a core point.

Three types of points:

  • Core point: Has at least min_samples points (including itself) within distance ε. This point sits in the dense interior of a cluster.
  • Border point: Within distance ε of a core point, but has fewer than min_samples in its own neighborhood. On the edge of a cluster.
  • Noise point (outlier): Neither a core point nor a border point. Gets label = −1.

The DBSCAN Algorithm

  1. Label every point as core, border, or noise using ε and min_samples.
  2. Connect core points that are within ε of each other (they form a cluster).
  3. Assign border points to a neighboring core point's cluster.
  4. All noise points are left unlabeled (−1).
💡 Plain-English Example: Core, Border, and Noise in a Grid

Set ε = 1.5 units, min_samples = 3. Imagine 9 points on a 2D grid:

Dense group: A(1,1), B(1,2), C(2,1), D(2,2) — all within 1.5 of each other.
Bridge point: E(3,2) — within 1.5 of D, but only D and C are in its neighborhood (2 points, less than min_samples=3).
Loner: F(8,8) — far from everything, only 1 point in its neighborhood.

A, B, C, D each have 3+ neighbors within ε → core points. They form Cluster 1.
E is within ε of core point D → border point. It joins Cluster 1 but cannot expand it.
F has no core point within ε → noise point, labeled −1 (outlier).

This is what makes DBSCAN powerful: it found the dense blob automatically and flagged F as an outlier without you having to specify K=1 beforehand.

Key Advantages over K-Means

  • Does not require specifying K in advance — the number of clusters is determined automatically
  • Can find arbitrarily shaped clusters (not just spherical)
  • Explicitly identifies outliers — K-Means forces every point into a cluster
  • Not sensitive to outliers pulling centroids (K-Means is very sensitive)
💡 Core, Border, Noise — 8 Points, ε=1.5, min_samples=3

Picture 8 job postings plotted on a 2D salary/experience axis (coordinates simplified). Set ε=1.5 (neighborhood radius) and min_samples=3 (need at least 3 neighbors to be a "core" point).

PointNeighbors within ε=1.5CountType
AB, C (+ itself)3Core — dense interior
BA, C (+ itself)3Core
CA, B (+ itself)3Core
DE, F (+ itself)3Core
ED (+ itself)2Border — within ε of D (a core), but not dense enough itself
FD (+ itself)2Border
Gonly itself1Noise (−1) — isolated point, no cluster
Honly itself1Noise (−1)

Result: DBSCAN finds 2 clusters: Cluster 0 = {A, B, C, E, F} (E and F get pulled in because they're within ε of core point D — wait, D is in this cluster too). Actually Cluster 0 = {A,B,C} and Cluster 1 = {D,E,F}. Points G and H are labeled −1 (outliers).

Key insight: K-Means would have forced G and H into some cluster. DBSCAN says "these don't belong anywhere" — they're genuine outliers (maybe data entry errors or exotic job postings).

Tuning tip: If ε is too small, almost every point becomes noise. If ε is too large, everything merges into one cluster. The k-NN distance plot below finds the right middle ground.

Choosing ε and min_samples

The standard heuristic: plot the k-nearest-neighbor distance for each point, sorted ascending. The "knee" in this plot suggests a good ε. min_samples is usually set to 2 × number_of_features or at least 5.

from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

# ── k-NN distance plot for choosing epsilon ───────────────────────
k = 5   # min_samples candidate
nbrs = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(X_scaled)
distances, _ = nbrs.kneighbors(X_scaled)
knn_dists = np.sort(distances[:, k-1])  # k-th nearest neighbor distance

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.plot(knn_dists, color='steelblue', lw=1.5)
ax.axhline(y=0.4, color='tomato', linestyle='--', lw=1.5, label='Suggested ε ≈ 0.4')
ax.set_xlabel('Points (sorted by k-NN distance)')
ax.set_ylabel(f'{k}-NN Distance')
ax.set_title('k-NN Distance Plot for DBSCAN Epsilon Selection')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_06_knn_dist.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

# ── Fit DBSCAN ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.4, min_samples=5)
db_labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_scaled)

n_clusters_db = len(set(db_labels)) - (1 if -1 in db_labels else 0)
n_noise_db    = np.sum(db_labels == -1)

print(f"DBSCAN found {n_clusters_db} clusters")
print(f"Noise points (outliers): {n_noise_db} ({100*n_noise_db/len(db_labels):.1f}%)")
print(f"Cluster sizes: {pd.Series(db_labels[db_labels != -1]).value_counts().to_dict()}")

# Silhouette score (only on non-noise points; need at least 2 clusters)
if n_clusters_db >= 2:
    mask_valid = db_labels != -1
    db_sil = silhouette_score(X_scaled[mask_valid], db_labels[mask_valid])
    print(f"Silhouette (non-noise only): {db_sil:.4f}")

# ── Visualize DBSCAN ─────────────────────────────────────────────
data['cluster_db'] = db_labels
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
colors_db = ['#7c8ff5','#56d9b0','#f59e45','#f56b6b','#c084fc']

for label in sorted(set(db_labels)):
    mask  = db_labels == label
    color = '#888888' if label == -1 else colors_db[label % len(colors_db)]
    name  = 'Noise (outlier)' if label == -1 else f'Cluster {label}'
    alpha = 0.3 if label == -1 else 0.7
    ms    = 20 if label == -1 else 30
    ax.scatter(data.loc[mask, 'years_exp'], data.loc[mask, 'salary'],
               c=color, alpha=alpha, s=ms, label=name)
ax.set_xlabel('Years of Experience')
ax.set_ylabel('Salary ($)')
ax.set_title('DBSCAN Clustering (ε=0.4, min_samples=5)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_07_dbscan.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

6.11 PCA — Dimensionality Reduction AN306

As the number of features grows, two problems emerge: (1) visualizing clusters becomes impossible beyond 3 dimensions, and (2) the "curse of dimensionality" makes distance-based clustering less effective. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projects high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space while retaining as much variance as possible.

What PCA Does

PCA finds a new set of axes — the principal components (PCs) — that are:

  • Linear combinations of the original features
  • Orthogonal to each other (uncorrelated)
  • Ordered by variance explained: PC1 captures the most variance, PC2 the second most, and so on
PC1 = w₁₁x₁ + w₁₂x₂ + … + w₁ₙxₙ (direction of maximum variance) PC2 = w₂₁x₁ + w₂₂x₂ + … + w₂ₙxₙ (orthogonal to PC1; second-most variance)
💡 What PCA Loadings Actually Mean

Say you have two features: salary (scaled) and years_exp (scaled). PCA might find:

PC1 = 0.71 × salary + 0.71 × years_exp

This is a "career achievement" axis — PC1 is high when both salary AND experience are high. A senior engineer with high salary and 12 years gets a large PC1 score. A new grad with low salary and 1 year gets a small one.

PC2 = 0.71 × salary − 0.71 × years_exp

PC2 captures the gap between salary and experience. High salary but low experience = positive PC2 (overachiever). Low salary but high experience = negative PC2 (underearner). The 0.71 and −0.71 are what appear in the loadings table from your PCA.

The weights w are called loadings. They tell you how much each original feature contributes to each PC.

When to Use PCA in Clustering

  • Visualization: Reduce to 2D or 3D to plot clusters
  • Noise reduction: Lower-variance components often capture noise; dropping them can improve cluster quality
  • Speed: Fewer dimensions means faster distance calculations for large datasets
⚠ Scale Before PCA
PCA is based on variance. If features have different scales, PCA will be dominated by the high-variance features — the same problem as with K-Means distances. Always StandardScaler → PCA → KMeans, in that order.

Implementation

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

# ── Fit PCA on scaled data ────────────────────────────────────────
pca = PCA()   # keep all components first to inspect explained variance
pca.fit(X_scaled)

# Explained variance ratio
evr = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
print("Explained Variance by Component:")
cumulative = 0
for i, ev in enumerate(evr):
    cumulative += ev
    print(f"  PC{i+1}: {ev*100:.1f}%  (cumulative: {cumulative*100:.1f}%)")

# ── Scree plot ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
axes[0].bar(range(1, len(evr)+1), evr*100, color='steelblue')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Principal Component')
axes[0].set_ylabel('% Variance Explained')
axes[0].set_title('Scree Plot — Individual Variance')
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

cumulative_evr = np.cumsum(evr)
axes[1].plot(range(1, len(evr)+1), cumulative_evr*100, 'o-', color='#56d9b0', lw=2)
axes[1].axhline(y=95, color='tomato', linestyle='--', lw=1.5, label='95% threshold')
axes[1].axhline(y=80, color='orange', linestyle='--', lw=1.5, label='80% threshold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Number of Components')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Cumulative % Variance Explained')
axes[1].set_title('Cumulative Explained Variance')
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_08_pca_scree.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

# ── Reduce to 2D for visualization ───────────────────────────────
pca2 = PCA(n_components=2)
X_pca = pca2.fit_transform(X_scaled)
print(f"\\nPCA 2D: captures {sum(pca2.explained_variance_ratio_)*100:.1f}% of variance")

# Re-run K-Means on PCA-reduced data
km_pca = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels_pca = km_pca.fit_predict(X_pca)

# 2D cluster plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
colors = ['#7c8ff5', '#56d9b0', '#f59e45']
for k in range(3):
    mask = labels_pca == k
    ax.scatter(X_pca[mask, 0], X_pca[mask, 1],
               c=colors[k], alpha=0.7, s=40, label=f'Cluster {k}')
ax.scatter(km_pca.cluster_centers_[:,0], km_pca.cluster_centers_[:,1],
           c='white', marker='X', s=250, zorder=5, edgecolors='gray', label='Centroids')
ax.set_xlabel(f'PC1 ({pca2.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.1f}% variance)')
ax.set_ylabel(f'PC2 ({pca2.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.1f}% variance)')
ax.set_title('K-Means on PCA-Reduced Data (2 Components)')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_09_pca_clusters.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

# ── PCA loadings — which original features drive each PC? ─────────
loadings = pd.DataFrame(pca2.components_.T,
                         columns=['PC1','PC2'],
                         index=data.columns[:3])  # original feature names
print("\\nPCA Loadings (contribution of each feature to each PC):")
print(loadings.round(3))

6.12 Cluster Profiling & Interpretation AN306 AN300

Fitting K-Means and getting cluster labels is only halfway. The other half — and the part that matters for a P4 presentation — is profiling each cluster: understanding what characterizes it, naming it, and explaining what it represents in business terms.

Statistical Profiling

# ── Profile clusters with descriptive statistics ──────────────────
# Use original (unscaled) data with cluster labels attached
profile = data.groupby('cluster')[['salary','years_exp','skill_score']].agg(
    ['mean','median','std','count']
)
print("Cluster Profiles:")
print(profile.round(1))

# Cleaner single-level column format
profile_summary = data.groupby('cluster').agg(
    count        = ('salary', 'count'),
    salary_mean  = ('salary', 'mean'),
    salary_std   = ('salary', 'std'),
    exp_mean     = ('years_exp', 'mean'),
    skill_mean   = ('skill_score', 'mean')
).round(1)
print("\\nCluster Summary:")
print(profile_summary)

Radar Charts for Multi-Dimensional Comparison

# Radar chart: compare clusters across all features simultaneously
# Normalize centroids to [0,1] for the radar axes
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch
import matplotlib

n_vars  = 3
features = ['salary', 'years_exp', 'skill_score']
angles   = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, n_vars, endpoint=False).tolist()
angles  += angles[:1]   # close the polygon

# Normalize each feature 0–1 for the radar
feat_data = data.groupby('cluster')[features].mean()
feat_norm = (feat_data - feat_data.min()) / (feat_data.max() - feat_data.min())

colors_r = ['#7c8ff5', '#56d9b0', '#f59e45']
fig, ax  = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8), subplot_kw=dict(polar=True))

for k, row in feat_norm.iterrows():
    vals = row.tolist() + row.tolist()[:1]
    ax.plot(angles, vals, 'o-', lw=2, color=colors_r[k], label=f'Cluster {k}')
    ax.fill(angles, vals, alpha=0.1, color=colors_r[k])

ax.set_xticks(angles[:-1])
ax.set_xticklabels(features, fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Cluster Radar Chart', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', pad=20)
ax.legend(loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.3, 1.1))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_10_radar.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Box Plots by Cluster

# Box plots show within-cluster spread, not just means
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 5))
features_plot = ['salary', 'years_exp', 'skill_score']
ylabels = ['Salary ($)', 'Years Exp', 'Skill Score']
colors_bp = ['#7c8ff5', '#56d9b0', '#f59e45']

for i, (feat, ylabel) in enumerate(zip(features_plot, ylabels)):
    groups = [data.loc[data['cluster']==k, feat] for k in range(3)]
    bp = axes[i].boxplot(groups, patch_artist=True, notch=False)
    for patch, color in zip(bp['boxes'], colors_bp):
        patch.set_facecolor(color)
        patch.set_alpha(0.7)
    axes[i].set_xticklabels([f'Cluster {k}' for k in range(3)])
    axes[i].set_ylabel(ylabel)
    axes[i].set_title(f'{feat.replace("_"," ").title()} by Cluster')
    axes[i].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('06_11_boxplots.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Naming the Clusters

After profiling, give each cluster a business-relevant label. This is the interpretive step that transforms a technical output ("Cluster 2") into an insight ("Senior Cloud Specialists"). The naming should be grounded in the actual statistics, not just intuition.

# Example naming based on profile statistics
cluster_names = {
    0: 'Entry-Level Generalists  (low salary, low exp, low skill)',
    1: 'Mid-Level Practitioners  (mid salary, ~5yr exp, mid skill)',
    2: 'Senior Specialists       (high salary, 12+ yr exp, high skill)'
}

data['cluster_name'] = data['cluster'].map(cluster_names)
print("\\nCluster Labels:")
print(data['cluster_name'].value_counts())

6.13 Cluster Stability — Adjusted Rand Index AN306

How confident should you be that your clusters are real and stable — not just artifacts of random initialization or the specific K chosen? The Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) measures agreement between two sets of cluster labels.

When You Have Ground Truth Labels

ARI compares a predicted clustering to a known ground truth:

ARI = (RI − E[RI]) / (max(RI) − E[RI])
  • ARI = 1.0: Perfect agreement — predicted clusters match ground truth exactly
  • ARI ≈ 0: Random agreement — no better than chance
  • ARI < 0: Systematic disagreement (worse than random)
💡 Plain-English Example: What ARI Actually Measures

Say you have 6 employees and you know their true department: {Alice, Bob} = Engineering; {Carol, Dan} = Marketing; {Eve, Frank} = Sales.

Your clustering predicts: Cluster 0 = {Alice, Bob}, Cluster 1 = {Carol, Dan}, Cluster 2 = {Eve, Frank}.
Every pair that belongs together is grouped together, every pair that shouldn't be is kept apart. ARI = 1.0 — perfect.

A second clustering predicts: Cluster 0 = {Alice, Carol, Eve}, Cluster 1 = {Bob, Dan, Frank}.
This just split everyone by some random pattern. The pairs that are co-grouped barely resemble the true structure. ARI ≈ 0 — no better than random.

ARI for stability testing: Run K-Means 20 times with different random seeds. If ARI between any two runs is 0.95+, the algorithm keeps finding the same clusters → the structure is real. If ARI between runs is 0.3, the clusters are unstable — the data doesn't have clear natural groups, and K is probably wrong.

Using ARI to Test Stability (Bootstrap)

from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

# ── Stability test: run K-Means 20 times with different seeds ────
# Measure how often different runs agree with each other
n_runs = 20
all_labels = []

for seed in range(n_runs):
    km_run = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init='k-means++', n_init=1, random_state=seed)
    all_labels.append(km_run.fit_predict(X_scaled))

# Compute pairwise ARI between all runs
ari_matrix = np.zeros((n_runs, n_runs))
for i in range(n_runs):
    for j in range(n_runs):
        ari_matrix[i,j] = adjusted_rand_score(all_labels[i], all_labels[j])

print(f"Mean pairwise ARI across {n_runs} runs: {ari_matrix[np.triu_indices(n_runs,1)].mean():.4f}")
print(f"Min  pairwise ARI: {ari_matrix[np.triu_indices(n_runs,1)].min():.4f}")
print("ARI close to 1.0 → stable clusters; ARI < 0.5 → unstable, reconsider K")

# ── Example: comparing K-Means vs. Agglomerative ──────────────────
ari_vs_agg = adjusted_rand_score(kmeans.labels_, agg_labels)
print(f"\\nARI (K-Means vs. Agglomerative): {ari_vs_agg:.4f}")
print("High ARI between methods = both algorithms agree on the structure")

6.14 Choosing a Clustering Algorithm AN306 AN300

AlgorithmStrengthsWeaknessesUse When
K-Means Fast; scalable; interpretable centroids; works well with large n Requires specifying K; assumes spherical clusters; sensitive to outliers and scaling Large datasets; clusters expected to be roughly spherical; speed is a priority; P4 default
Hierarchical (Ward) No K needed upfront; dendrogram gives full picture; deterministic O(n² log n) — slow for large n; memory intensive; must commit to K at the cut Smaller datasets (<10,000); want to visually inspect cluster hierarchy; exploring K
DBSCAN No K needed; finds arbitrary shapes; labels outliers; not sensitive to outlier points pulling centroids Hard to tune ε and min_samples; struggles with varying density; poorly defined silhouette for noise points Anomaly detection; clusters of irregular shapes; outlier labeling is a goal
✓ Recommended P4 Workflow
1. Scale with StandardScaler. 2. Run K-Means with elbow + silhouette to find K. 3. Fit K-Means with the best K. 4. If the dataset is small enough (<5000 rows), also run hierarchical clustering and compare dendrograms. 5. Profile every cluster with means, box plots, and a radar chart. 6. Name and present each cluster with business interpretation.

### ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering, DBSCAN
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

# ── CELL 1: Load and inspect job posting data ─────────────────────
df = pd.read_csv('job_postings.csv')
print(f"Shape: {df.shape}")
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.head())

# ── CELL 2: Select and clean features ─────────────────────────────

            'company_size', 'num_skills_required']
# (adjust to actual column names in your dataset)

cluster_df = df[features].dropna()
print(f"After dropping NaN: {cluster_df.shape[0]} rows")

X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(cluster_df)

# ── CELL 3: Elbow + Silhouette to find K ─────────────────────────
inertias, sil_scores = [], []
K_range = range(2, 11)

for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
    lbls = km.fit_predict(X)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    sil_scores.append(silhouette_score(X, lbls))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
axes[0].plot(K_range, inertias, 'o-', color='steelblue', lw=2)
axes[0].set_title('Elbow Method'); axes[0].set_xlabel('K'); axes[0].set_ylabel('Inertia')
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
axes[1].plot(K_range, sil_scores, 'o-', color='#56d9b0', lw=2)

axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

best_k = K_range[np.argmax(sil_scores)]
print(f"Best K by silhouette: {best_k}  (score={max(sil_scores):.4f})")

# ── CELL 4: Fit final model ───────────────────────────────────────
final_km = KMeans(n_clusters=best_k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
cluster_df = cluster_df.copy()
cluster_df['cluster'] = final_km.fit_predict(X)
df.loc[cluster_df.index, 'cluster'] = cluster_df['cluster']

# ── CELL 5: PCA visualization ─────────────────────────────────────
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_2d = pca.fit_transform(X)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
colors = ['#7c8ff5','#56d9b0','#f59e45','#f56b6b','#c084fc']
for k in range(best_k):

    ax.scatter(X_2d[mask,0], X_2d[mask,1], c=colors[k%5], alpha=0.6, s=30, label=f'Cluster {k}')
ax.set_title(f'K-Means K={best_k} — PCA Visualization')

ax.set_ylabel(f'PC2 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.1f}% var)')
ax.legend(); ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# ── CELL 6: Profile and name clusters ────────────────────────────

Part 7 — Association Rule Analysis

From market baskets to actionable rules — support, confidence, lift, Apriori, and mlxtend from scratch

7.1 Why Association Rules?

AN300 AN306

Clustering (Part 6) grouped similar observations. Association rule mining groups items that co-occur in the same transaction. The canonical application is market basket analysis: given millions of shopping receipts, find which products are bought together.

The Core Question

If a customer buys diapers, how likely are they also to buy beer? The legendary "diapers and beer" finding from Walmart's data in the 1990s is often cited as the first real win of association rule mining — parents stocking up on diapers apparently also bought beer for the weekend. That insight drove shelf placement decisions.

More formally, an association rule has the form:

Association Rule Notation {Antecedent} → {Consequent}
e.g., {diapers, formula} → {beer}

The antecedent is the "if" side; the consequent is the "then" side. The rule does not imply causation — it means these items appear together in transactions more often than chance would predict.

Use Cases Beyond Retail

  • Streaming platforms — "Users who watched X also watched Y"
  • Healthcare — "Patients with diagnosis A and B frequently also receive treatment C"
  • Web analytics — "Pages visited together in the same session"
  • Cybersecurity — "Events that co-occur in attack sequences"
  • Banking — "Clients who hold product A and B also open product C"

Transaction Data Format

The raw data is a list of transactions. Each transaction is a set of items (the basket). There is no numerical target variable y — this is unsupervised, like clustering.

# Example transactions — each row is one receipt
Transaction 1: {milk, bread, eggs}
Transaction 2: {milk, diapers, beer, cereal}
Transaction 3: {bread, diapers, beer, cereal}
Transaction 4: {milk, bread, diapers, beer}
Transaction 5: {bread, cereal}
Key distinction from clustering: In clustering, every observation has feature columns (height, weight, income…). In association rule mining, the "features" are binary item indicators — an item is either in the basket or not. The dataset is typically very sparse (most items are absent from any given transaction).

The Vocabulary

  • Item — an individual product, page, event, etc.
  • Itemset — any subset of items (e.g., {milk, bread})
  • Transaction — one basket/receipt containing a set of items
  • k-itemset — an itemset of size k (a 2-itemset has two items)
  • Frequent itemset — an itemset whose support ≥ min_support threshold

7.2 Support, Confidence, and Lift — The Three Core Metrics

AN300 AN306

Three numbers describe every association rule. You need all three — no single metric is sufficient.

Support

Support measures how common an itemset is. It is the fraction of all transactions that contain the itemset.

Support of Itemset A support(A) = count(transactions containing A) / total transactions

Support applies to any itemset, not just rules. For the rule A → B:

Support of Rule A → B support(A → B) = support(A ∪ B) = count(A and B together) / N

Using the five transactions above, let's compute support for {diapers}:

  • Transactions containing diapers: T2, T3, T4 → count = 3
  • Total transactions: N = 5
  • support({diapers}) = 3/5 = 0.60
Low support = unreliable rule. A rule might appear to have perfect confidence while being based on only 2 transactions. Setting a minimum support threshold filters out rules that are statistically noise — they happened to co-occur once or twice by chance.
🔑 Why low support rules are dangerous — a concrete example:
Suppose you have 10,000 transactions. You find the rule {wasabi} → {soy sauce} with confidence = 1.0 and support = 0.0003 (3 transactions). Three people bought both items. Perfect confidence — yes, those 3 all bought soy sauce too. But is this actionable? Should you reorganize your store based on 3 customers?

Compare to {bread} → {butter} with confidence = 0.68 and support = 0.12 (1,200 transactions). Less than "perfect" confidence, but based on 1,200 real co-purchases. The bread/butter insight is actionable. The wasabi insight is noise that happens to look perfect.

Rule of thumb: In a dataset of 10,000 transactions, min_support = 0.01 means a rule needs to appear in at least 100 transactions before you trust it. Start there, then lower it if you need rarer patterns.

Confidence

Confidence measures how reliable the rule is, given that the antecedent occurred. It is a conditional probability:

Confidence of A → B confidence(A → B) = support(A ∪ B) / support(A) = P(B | A)

Confidence is "if someone bought A, what fraction of the time did they also buy B?"

Example: rule {diapers} → {beer}

  • Transactions with both diapers AND beer: T2, T3, T4 → count = 3, support = 3/5 = 0.60
  • Transactions with diapers only: T2, T3, T4 → support = 3/5 = 0.60
  • confidence({diapers} → {beer}) = 0.60 / 0.60 = 1.00

Perfect confidence! Every time diapers appear, beer appears too in this tiny dataset.

Confidence is a conditional probability, not joint probability. confidence(A → B) ≠ confidence(B → A). A rule and its reverse can have wildly different confidences. If confidence(A → B) = 0.9, that tells you nothing about confidence(B → A).

Lift

Lift is the most important of the three for actionability. It measures how much more often A and B co-occur than expected if they were independent.

Lift of A → B lift(A → B) = confidence(A → B) / support(B) = support(A ∪ B) / (support(A) × support(B))

Interpretation:

  • lift = 1 → A and B are independent; knowing A tells you nothing about B
  • lift > 1 → A and B co-occur more than chance; positive association
  • lift < 1 → A and B co-occur less than chance; negative association (substitutes)

Example: rule {diapers} → {beer}

  • confidence({diapers} → {beer}) = 1.00
  • support({beer}) = count(T2,T3,T4)/5 = 3/5 = 0.60
  • lift = 1.00 / 0.60 = 1.667

Beer appears with diapers 1.67× more often than it appears generally. That's a meaningful positive association.

💡 Lift Removes the Base Rate — Why We Can't Use Confidence Alone
Imagine "whole milk" appears in 25% of all baskets. Any customer buying anything has a 25% baseline chance of also having milk. So a rule that gets confidence = 0.25 for milk is actually worthless — it's just the base rate.

Lift fixes this by dividing out that baseline (support of the consequent):
RuleConfidencesupport(milk) = 0.25LiftMeaning
{random item} → {milk}0.25÷ 0.251.00No real association — just the base rate
{cereal} → {milk}0.38÷ 0.251.5252% more likely than chance — real signal
{cereal, yogurt} → {milk}0.55÷ 0.252.20Dairy shoppers strongly co-purchase milk
{non-dairy creamer} → {milk}0.10÷ 0.250.4060% less likely — a substitute, not complement
Key insight: Confidence = 0.38 looks mediocre until you realize the baseline is only 0.25. Lift = 1.52 reveals the genuine association. The non-dairy creamer row (lift = 0.40) also reveals a negative association — people buying creamer are less likely to also buy milk, which you'd never see from confidence alone.
Lift is symmetric: lift(A → B) = lift(B → A). Support is also symmetric. Confidence is NOT symmetric. This asymmetry is why you should always examine both directions of a rule.

Putting It Together

MetricMeasuresRangeThreshold
SupportFrequency / prevalence of the itemset0 to 1min_support (e.g., 0.01–0.05)
ConfidenceReliability of rule, given antecedent0 to 1min_confidence (e.g., 0.5–0.8)
LiftStrength of association vs. independence0 to ∞lift > 1 (meaningful); > 1.5 (strong)
Rule of thumb for minimum thresholds:
With millions of transactions (e-commerce), min_support as low as 0.001 (0.1%) can still catch important patterns. With hundreds of transactions (small survey), you might need 0.1 (10%) to avoid noise. Always tune thresholds to your domain. Confidence ≥ 0.5 and lift ≥ 1.0 are common starting points.

Additional Metrics: Conviction and Leverage

Two other metrics you may encounter:

Leverage

leverage(A → B) = support(A ∪ B) − support(A) × support(B)

Measures how much more co-occurrence there is than expected under independence. Zero means independence. Ranges from −1 to 1. Similar story to lift, but in additive rather than ratio form. mlxtend computes it.

Conviction

conviction(A → B) = (1 − support(B)) / (1 − confidence(A → B))

Measures how often the rule makes an incorrect prediction. High conviction = rule rarely fails. Ranges from 0 to ∞; conviction = 1 means independence; ∞ means perfect confidence (rule never wrong in one direction). Less commonly used than lift.

💡 Conviction by Hand — Why the Formula Goes to Infinity
Using a tiny 5-transaction dataset where {diapers} → {beer} holds perfectly (every diaper purchase includes beer), and support(beer) = 0.60:

conviction = (1 − support(B)) / (1 − confidence)

Perfect rule — diapers → beer (confidence = 1.00, support(beer) = 0.60)
conviction = (1 − 0.60) / (1 − 1.00) = 0.40 / 0.00 = ∞
Every single diaper transaction in our data also contains beer — zero failures. When confidence = 1.0, the denominator (1 − 1.0) = 0, and dividing by zero signals "this rule has zero failures," which is represented as infinity.

Moderate rule — bread → cereal (confidence = 0.75, support(cereal) = 0.60)
conviction = (1 − 0.60) / (1 − 0.75) = 0.40 / 0.25 = 1.60
This rule is 60% better than random. At conviction = 1.0, bread and cereal would be independent (knowing someone bought bread tells you nothing about cereal). Conviction = 1.60 means the rule performs better than that baseline.

Quick reference: conviction = 1 → independence (no predictive value); conviction > 1 → rule beats random; conviction = ∞ → perfect rule (confidence = 1.0, never fails).

7.3 The Apriori Algorithm — How Frequent Itemsets Are Found

AN300 AN306

Brute force is impossible. If a retailer sells 10,000 products, the number of possible itemsets is 2^10,000 — astronomically large. The Apriori algorithm uses a clever pruning strategy to explore only promising itemsets.

The Apriori Property (Anti-Monotonicity)

Key insight: If an itemset is infrequent (below min_support), then every superset of that itemset is also infrequent.

Equivalently: if an itemset is frequent, then every subset of it is also frequent.
🔑 Why this pruning makes sense — the umbrella logic:
Think about it this way: if only 5 out of 1,000 people bought {milk AND beer AND diapers}, then it's impossible for more than 5 people to have bought {milk AND beer AND diapers AND wipes}. The 4-item set can only be a subset of the 3-item set's transactions.

So if {milk, beer} is rare (say, 2% of baskets), there's zero point checking {milk, beer, diapers}, {milk, beer, wipes}, {milk, beer, cereal} — they can only be rarer. We skip them all. With a store selling 10,000 products, this pruning eliminates billions of combinations instantly.

This lets us prune the search space dramatically. If {milk, beer} is infrequent, we don't need to check {milk, beer, diapers}, {milk, beer, bread}, etc. We prune the entire branch.

The Algorithm — Step by Step

1
Generate 1-itemsets (k=1). Count how often each individual item appears. Keep only those with support ≥ min_support. This is the set of frequent 1-itemsets L₁.
2
Generate candidate k+1-itemsets by joining. Combine pairs of frequent k-itemsets that share the first k−1 items (lexicographic join). For k=1, every pair of frequent items forms a candidate 2-itemset.
3
Prune candidates using Apriori property. Any candidate k-itemset whose (k−1)-item subsets are NOT all frequent is pruned immediately without counting. This prevents unnecessary database scans.
4
Scan database to count surviving candidates. Compute support for each surviving candidate by scanning all transactions. Keep only those with support ≥ min_support. These are Lₖ.
5
Repeat until no new frequent itemsets found. Increment k and repeat from Step 2. Stop when no new candidates can be generated.
6
Generate rules from all frequent itemsets. For each frequent itemset F with |F| ≥ 2, generate all possible A → (F − A) rules where A ⊂ F. Keep those with confidence ≥ min_confidence (and optionally min_lift).

Worked Example — 5 Transactions

Using the 5 transactions from Module 7.1 with min_support = 0.6 (3/5 transactions):

Step 1 — Frequent 1-itemsets L₁

ItemCountSupportFrequent?
milk30.60✓ Yes
bread40.80✓ Yes
eggs10.20✗ No
diapers30.60✓ Yes
beer30.60✓ Yes
cereal30.60✓ Yes

L₁ = {milk, bread, diapers, beer, cereal}. Eggs dropped (support 0.20 < 0.60).

Step 2 — Candidate 2-itemsets C₂ (join L₁ with itself)

All pairs from L₁: {milk,bread}, {milk,diapers}, {milk,beer}, {milk,cereal}, {bread,diapers}, {bread,beer}, {bread,cereal}, {diapers,beer}, {diapers,cereal}, {beer,cereal} — 10 candidates. All subsets of size 1 are in L₁, so none pruned yet. Count each by scanning transactions.

Step 3 — Frequent 2-itemsets L₂ (keep support ≥ 0.60)

2-itemsetCountSupportFrequent?
{milk, bread}20.40✗
{milk, diapers}20.40✗
{milk, beer}20.40✗
{milk, cereal}10.20✗
{bread, diapers}20.40✗
{bread, beer}20.40✗
{bread, cereal}30.60✓
{diapers, beer}30.60✓
{diapers, cereal}20.40✗
{beer, cereal}20.40✗

L₂ = {{bread,cereal}, {diapers,beer}}. For 3-itemsets, we'd need pairs from L₂ that share one item — but {bread,cereal} and {diapers,beer} share no items, so C₃ = ∅. Algorithm terminates.

Generate Rules from L₂

From {diapers, beer} (support = 0.60), min_confidence = 0.60:

  • diapers → beer: conf = 0.60/0.60 = 1.00 ✓, lift = 1.00/0.60 = 1.67
  • beer → diapers: conf = 0.60/0.60 = 1.00 ✓, lift = 1.00/0.60 = 1.67

From {bread, cereal} (support = 0.60):

  • bread → cereal: conf = 0.60/0.80 = 0.75 ✓, lift = 0.75/0.60 = 1.25
  • cereal → bread: conf = 0.60/0.60 = 1.00 ✓, lift = 1.00/0.80 = 1.25

Time Complexity

Apriori must scan the full database once per itemset level k. With large datasets or low min_support, this is slow. The number of database scans = max itemset length. For large datasets, FP-Growth (Module 7.7) is preferred.

7.4 mlxtend Implementation — Full Python Workflow

AN306 AN300

Python's mlxtend library implements Apriori and FP-Growth for us. The workflow has three stages: encode the data, mine frequent itemsets, then generate rules.

Installing mlxtend

pip install mlxtend

Stage 1 — Encode Transactions into One-Hot Format

mlxtend requires a one-hot encoded DataFrame (also called the transaction matrix): each row is a transaction, each column is an item, cell = True/False (item in basket or not).

import pandas as pd
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules

# Raw transactions — list of lists
transactions = [
    ['milk', 'bread', 'eggs'],
    ['milk', 'diapers', 'beer', 'cereal'],
    ['bread', 'diapers', 'beer', 'cereal'],
    ['milk', 'bread', 'diapers', 'beer'],
    ['bread', 'cereal']
]

# Step 1: Fit TransactionEncoder
te = TransactionEncoder()
te_array = te.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)

# Step 2: Convert to DataFrame
df_te = pd.DataFrame(te_array, columns=te.columns_)
print(df_te)
#        beer  bread  cereal  diapers   eggs   milk
# 0     False   True   False    False   True   True
# 1      True  False    True     True  False   True
# 2      True   True    True     True  False  False
# 3      True   True   False     True  False   True
# 4     False   True    True    False  False  False

Stage 2 — Mine Frequent Itemsets with Apriori

# Step 3: Run Apriori to find frequent itemsets
frequent_itemsets = apriori(
    df_te,
    min_support=0.4,         # at least 40% of transactions
    use_colnames=True,       # use column names, not indices
    max_len=None             # no limit on itemset size
)

# Sort by support descending
frequent_itemsets.sort_values('support', ascending=False, inplace=True)
print(frequent_itemsets.head(10))
#    support         itemsets
# 0      0.8          (bread)
# 1      0.6         (cereal)
# 2      0.6        (diapers)
# ...
# 7      0.6  (bread, cereal)
# 8      0.6  (beer, diapers)

# Add itemset length column for filtering
frequent_itemsets['length'] = frequent_itemsets['itemsets'].apply(len)
print(frequent_itemsets[frequent_itemsets['length'] >= 2])
Important: apriori() returns itemsets as frozensets. You can't index them with [0]. Use list(itemset) to convert when needed. The use_colnames=True argument is essential — without it, columns are integer indices and the output is unreadable.

Stage 3 — Generate Association Rules

# Step 4: Generate rules from frequent itemsets
rules = association_rules(
    frequent_itemsets,
    metric="lift",           # filter by this metric
    min_threshold=1.0        # minimum value for the metric
)

# Key columns returned:
# antecedents, consequents — frozensets
# antecedent support, consequent support — individual support values
# support — joint support of the rule
# confidence — P(consequent | antecedent)
# lift — confidence / consequent support
# leverage — support - (ant_support * cons_support)
# conviction — (1 - cons_support) / (1 - confidence)

print(rules[['antecedents', 'consequents', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']].to_string())
#          antecedents    consequents  support  confidence      lift
# 0          (cereal)        (bread)      0.6        1.00   1.25000
# 1           (bread)       (cereal)      0.6        0.75   1.25000
# 2         (diapers)         (beer)      0.6        1.00   1.66667
# 3            (beer)       (diapers)     0.6        1.00   1.66667

Filtering Rules Programmatically

# Filter by multiple conditions
strong_rules = rules[
    (rules['confidence'] >= 0.7) &
    (rules['lift'] > 1.2) &
    (rules['support'] >= 0.05)
].copy()

# Sort by lift descending
strong_rules.sort_values('lift', ascending=False, inplace=True)
print(strong_rules.head(20))

# Count rules meeting criteria
print(f"Total rules found: {len(rules)}")
print(f"Strong rules (conf≥0.7, lift>1.2): {len(strong_rules)}")

Converting Frozensets to Readable Strings

# Pretty-print rules as "A → B" format
def rule_to_string(row):
    ant = ', '.join(sorted(row['antecedents']))
    cons = ', '.join(sorted(row['consequents']))
    return f"{ant} → {cons}"

strong_rules['rule'] = strong_rules.apply(rule_to_string, axis=1)
print(strong_rules[['rule', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']].to_string())

Visualizing Rule Space

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.cm as cm
import numpy as np

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# --- Plot 1: Support vs Confidence (colored by lift)
sc = axes[0].scatter(
    rules['support'], rules['confidence'],
    c=rules['lift'], cmap='RdYlGn',
    alpha=0.7, s=80, edgecolors='none'

plt.colorbar(sc, ax=axes[0], label='Lift')

# --- Plot 2: Top N rules by lift (horizontal bar chart)

top['rule'] = top.apply(rule_to_string, axis=1)

axes[1].barh(range(len(top)), top['lift'], color='#7c8ff5', alpha=0.85)

axes[1].set_yticklabels(top['rule'], fontsize=8)

Colab tip: With large datasets, apriori() can produce hundreds of thousands of rules. Always start with high min_support and work down. Use max_len=3 to limit to 3-item rules first, then explore larger combinations selectively.

7.5 Interpreting Association Rules

AN300 AN306

Reading a Rule Completely

When you encounter a rule, report all three numbers, not just one:

# Example rule output:
# antecedents: (whole milk)
# consequents: (other vegetables)
# support:     0.0748   → 7.5% of all baskets contain both
# confidence:  0.4867   → 48.7% of whole-milk buyers also buy vegetables
# lift:        1.5136   → 51% more likely than independent chance

Translate in plain language: "Customers who buy whole milk also buy other vegetables nearly half the time — and they're 51% more likely to do so than a randomly selected customer."

The Confidence Trap

High confidence alone is not enough. If beer has 95% support (bought in almost every transaction), then ANY rule with beer as the consequent will have confidence near 95% — even a rule like {bubble wrap} → {beer} would be 95% confident! Lift corrects for this. A rule with confidence=0.80 and lift=0.9 is WORSE than one with confidence=0.50 and lift=2.1 — the first is weaker than expected given how common the consequent is.

Directionality Matters

Two rules can describe the same relationship but have very different confidence levels:

  • {premium whiskey} → {soda water}: conf = 0.80, lift = 2.3
  • {soda water} → {premium whiskey}: conf = 0.12, lift = 2.3 (same lift, low confidence — soda is very common)

The first rule drives action: "stock soda water next to premium whiskey." The second doesn't — most people buying soda water are not buying premium whiskey.

Actionability Criteria

A rule is actionable if:

  1. It's new information — {tea} → {milk} is obvious in British culture; not actionable
  2. It's large enough to matter — support above a business-meaningful threshold
  3. It's reliable — confidence high enough to act on without excessive misses
  4. The association is real — lift meaningfully above 1
  5. Action is possible — you can actually change shelf placement, offer bundles, trigger a recommendation

Interpreting Lift Values

Lift ValueInterpretationBusiness Implication
< 1Negative association (items avoid each other)Competing products; don't cross-promote
= 1Independence; no associationNo relationship to exploit
1.0 – 1.3Weak positive associationExists but marginally useful
1.3 – 2.0Moderate positive associationWorth testing in recommendation engine
2.0 – 5.0Strong positive associationHigh-value cross-sell opportunity
> 5.0Very strong associationNear-complementary products; bundle deals

7.6 Filtering, Ranking, and Selecting Rules

AN306

The Rule Explosion Problem

With real retail data (50,000+ transactions, 1,000+ products), Apriori with min_support=0.01 can generate millions of rules. You need a systematic approach to surface only the useful ones.

Strategy 1 — Multi-metric Filter

def filter_rules(rules_df, min_support=0.01, min_confidence=0.5,
                 min_lift=1.2, max_len_ant=3, max_len_cons=1):
    """
    Filter association rules by multiple criteria.

    Parameters
    ----------
    min_support    : minimum support of the full rule (A ∪ B)
    min_confidence : minimum confidence
    min_lift       : minimum lift (1.0 = independence; 1.2 = moderate filter)
    max_len_ant    : max number of items in antecedent
    max_len_cons   : max items in consequent (1 = simpler, more interpretable rules)
    """
    rules_df = rules_df.copy()
    rules_df['ant_len'] = rules_df['antecedents'].apply(len)
    rules_df['cons_len'] = rules_df['consequents'].apply(len)

    mask = (
        (rules_df['support']    >= min_support) &
        (rules_df['confidence'] >= min_confidence) &
        (rules_df['lift']       >= min_lift) &
        (rules_df['ant_len']   <= max_len_ant) &
        (rules_df['cons_len']  <= max_len_cons)
    )
    return rules_df[mask].sort_values('lift', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

filtered = filter_rules(rules, min_support=0.01, min_confidence=0.5, min_lift=1.5)
print(f"Filtered from {len(rules)} to {len(filtered)} rules")

Strategy 2 — Target-Item Search

When you want rules about a specific product (e.g., "what leads people to buy Product X?"):

def rules_for_item(rules_df, item, role='consequent'):
    """
    Find all rules where \`item\` appears in the specified role.

    role: 'consequent'  → "what leads to buying X?"
          'antecedent'  → "if someone buys X, what else do they buy?"
    """
    if role == 'consequent':
        mask = rules_df['consequents'].apply(lambda x: item in x)
    else:
        mask = rules_df['antecedents'].apply(lambda x: item in x)

    return rules_df[mask].sort_values('lift', ascending=False)

# "What other items predict beer purchases?"
beer_rules = rules_for_item(rules, 'beer', role='consequent')
print(beer_rules[['antecedents', 'consequents', 'confidence', 'lift']].head(10))

Strategy 3 — Diversity Filter (Deduplication)

Rules like {A} → {B} and {A, C} → {B} with similar lift are often redundant. The simpler rule (fewer antecedent items) is usually preferred for actionability. Sort by lift descending, then optionally deduplicate on consequent.

# Keep only the top rule per consequent (simplest, highest-lift)
top_per_consequent = (
    filtered
    .sort_values(['consequents', 'lift', 'ant_len'],
                 ascending=[True, False, True])
    .drop_duplicates(subset='consequents', keep='first')
)
print(top_per_consequent[['antecedents', 'consequents', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']])

Strategy 4 — Heatmap of Item Co-occurrence

Before running Apriori, a co-occurrence heatmap gives intuition about which items are worth exploring:

import seaborn as sns

# Build co-occurrence matrix from the one-hot DataFrame
# (df_te is the TransactionEncoder output)
cooccurrence = df_te.T.dot(df_te)  # item × item matrix, diagonal = item count
# Zero out diagonal (self-co-occurrence)
for col in cooccurrence.columns:
    cooccurrence.loc[col, col] = 0

# Normalize to co-occurrence rate (fraction of transactions)
n_transactions = len(df_te)
cooccurrence_rate = cooccurrence / n_transactions

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))
sns.heatmap(
    cooccurrence_rate,
    cmap='Blues', annot=False,
    xticklabels=True, yticklabels=True,
    linewidths=0.3
)
plt.title('Item Co-occurrence Rate (fraction of all transactions)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=8)
plt.yticks(rotation=0, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

7.7 FP-Growth — The Faster Alternative to Apriori

AN306

Why FP-Growth?

Apriori's weakness is the number of database scans — it scans the full transaction database once per itemset level. With millions of transactions, that's slow. FP-Growth (Frequent Pattern Growth) scans the database only twice and stores the data in a compact in-memory tree structure called the FP-tree.

How It Works (Conceptual)

1
First scan: Count support of all individual items. Discard infrequent ones. Sort remaining items by frequency descending.
2
Second scan: Build the FP-tree. Each transaction is inserted as a path from root to leaf, with shared prefixes merged. Each node stores the item name and its count along that path.
3
Mine the FP-tree: For each frequent item (starting from least frequent), extract all paths leading to it (called the conditional pattern base). Build a conditional FP-tree and mine it recursively. Each level produces frequent itemsets without additional database scans.

The result is identical to Apriori — the same set of frequent itemsets — but typically 10–100× faster on large data.

Using FP-Growth in mlxtend

from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import fpgrowth

# SAME interface as apriori — just swap the function
frequent_itemsets_fp = fpgrowth(
    df_te,
    min_support=0.01,
    use_colnames=True,
    max_len=None
)

# Generate rules identically
rules_fp = association_rules(
    frequent_itemsets_fp,
    metric="lift",
    min_threshold=1.0
)

print(f"Frequent itemsets (FP-Growth): {len(frequent_itemsets_fp)}")
print(f"Rules generated: {len(rules_fp)}")
When to use which:
Apriori — small datasets (≤10,000 transactions), educational settings, when you want to trace the pruning logic step by step.
FP-Growth — real production scenarios, datasets >10,000 transactions, when speed matters. Use fpgrowth by default and fall back to apriori only for debugging or teaching.

7.8 Common Mistakes and Exam Traps

AN300
Trap 1 — Confidence does not equal predictive accuracy. High confidence for A → B means "when A occurs, B occurs often." It says nothing about what happens when A does NOT occur. It is NOT accuracy in the classification sense. Association rules are not classifiers.
Trap 2 — Support is symmetric, confidence is not. support(A → B) = support(B → A) always. confidence(A → B) ≠ confidence(B → A) in general. Lift is symmetric: lift(A → B) = lift(B → A) always.
Trap 3 — Apriori property is anti-monotone for support, not confidence. The anti-monotone pruning rule — "if infrequent, all supersets infrequent" — applies to support only. Confidence does not follow this property. You cannot prune candidate itemsets based on the confidence of their subsets.
Trap 4 — min_support must be set before rules are generated. You cannot retroactively lower min_support after calling apriori() and expect to find more rules. Apriori prunes itemsets during the mining phase. If you lower min_support, you must re-run apriori() from scratch. The frequent_itemsets DataFrame only contains itemsets that met the original threshold.
Trap 5 — lift = 1 does not mean "no co-occurrence." Items with lift = 1 DO co-occur in some transactions. It means they co-occur at EXACTLY the rate you'd expect if they were independent. Items that never co-occur have support(A ∪ B) = 0 and confidence = 0, but lift is undefined (division by zero). mlxtend will return NaN for those.
Trap 6 — Association rules do not imply causation. Diapers and beer co-occurring doesn't mean buying diapers causes beer purchase (or vice versa). Both may be driven by a confounding variable (new parents restocking on a weekend). Association mining finds co-occurrence patterns, not causal mechanisms. Never interpret a rule as "buying A causes buying B."
Trap 7 — Lowering min_support is exponential in cost. Halving min_support can more than double (sometimes 10×) the number of frequent itemsets. The relationship is not linear. Always check item count and expected rule count before running with very low thresholds on large data.

Choosing min_support in Practice

Dataset SizeTypical min_supportRationale
< 100 transactions0.20 – 0.50High threshold needed to avoid noise
100 – 10,0000.05 – 0.20Standard range
10,000 – 1M0.01 – 0.05Even rare rules have enough occurrences
> 1M transactions0.001 – 0.01Very rare co-occurrences still statistically reliable

Lab 7 — Market Basket Analysis Lab

This lab uses the Groceries dataset (from the R arules package), a classic market basket analysis dataset of 9,835 grocery transactions. We'll mine frequent itemsets, generate rules, and interpret the most actionable findings.

Setup — Load and Inspect

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.cm as cm
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import fpgrowth, association_rules

# --- Load the Groceries dataset ---
# Option 1: Load from mlxtend's built-in datasets
# (not always available; use the CSV approach below)

# Option 2: Download from GitHub
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stedy/Machine-Learning-with-R-datasets/master/groceries.csv"
raw = pd.read_csv(url, header=None)

# Each row is one transaction (comma-separated items in one string)
# Split into lists
transactions = raw[0].str.split(',').tolist()
print(f"Number of transactions: {len(transactions)}")
print(f"Sample transaction: {transactions[0]}")
print(f"Sample transaction: {transactions[1]}")
# --- Basic statistics ---
lengths = [len(t) for t in transactions]
print(f"Mean basket size:   {np.mean(lengths):.2f}")
print(f"Median basket size: {np.median(lengths):.1f}")
print(f"Max basket size:    {max(lengths)}")
print(f"Min basket size:    {min(lengths)}")

# Item frequency
from collections import Counter
all_items = [item for transaction in transactions for item in transaction]
item_counts = Counter(all_items)
print(f"\\nTotal unique items: {len(item_counts)}")

# Most common items
top20 = pd.DataFrame(item_counts.most_common(20),
                     columns=['item', 'count'])
top20['support'] = top20['count'] / len(transactions)
print(top20)

Cell 2 — One-Hot Encode and Visualize Item Frequency

# --- Encode ---
te = TransactionEncoder()
te_array = te.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)
df_te = pd.DataFrame(te_array, columns=te.columns_)

print(f"One-hot matrix shape: {df_te.shape}")  # (9835, 169)

# --- Plot top 20 items by support ---
item_support = df_te.mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(20)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
bars = ax.barh(range(len(item_support)), item_support.values[::-1],
               color='#7c8ff5', alpha=0.85, edgecolor='none')
ax.set_yticks(range(len(item_support)))
ax.set_yticklabels(item_support.index[::-1])
ax.set_xlabel('Support (fraction of transactions)')
ax.set_title('Top 20 Items by Support — Groceries Dataset')
ax.axvline(x=0.1, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.6, label='support = 0.10')
ax.legend()

plt.savefig('item_frequency.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

print("Note: 'whole milk' appears in", f"{item_support['whole milk']:.1%}",
      "of all transactions — the most common single item.")

Cell 3 — Mine Frequent Itemsets with FP-Growth

# --- FP-Growth ---
frequent_itemsets = fpgrowth(
    df_te,
    min_support=0.01,    # 1% = at least ~98 of 9,835 transactions
    use_colnames=True,
    max_len=4            # limit to 4-item rules for speed
)

frequent_itemsets['length'] = frequent_itemsets['itemsets'].apply(len)
print(f"Frequent itemsets found: {len(frequent_itemsets)}")
print("\\nBreakdown by itemset length:")
print(frequent_itemsets['length'].value_counts().sort_index())

# Top 15 frequent 2-itemsets (most useful for rules)
top_pairs = (frequent_itemsets
             [frequent_itemsets['length'] == 2]
             .sort_values('support', ascending=False)
             .head(15))
print("\\nTop 15 frequent item pairs:")
print(top_pairs[['support', 'itemsets']].to_string())

Cell 4 — Generate and Filter Association Rules

# --- Generate rules ---
rules = association_rules(
    frequent_itemsets,
    metric="confidence",
    min_threshold=0.3    # start broad, we'll filter
)

print(f"Total rules generated: {len(rules)}")
print(f"Rules with lift > 1:   {(rules['lift'] > 1).sum()}")
print(f"Rules with lift > 2:   {(rules['lift'] > 2).sum()}")
print(f"Rules with lift > 3:   {(rules['lift'] > 3).sum()}")

# --- Apply multi-metric filter ---
strong_rules = rules[
    (rules['confidence'] >= 0.50) &
    (rules['lift']       >= 2.00) &
    (rules['support']    >= 0.01)
].copy()

strong_rules['ant_len'] = strong_rules['antecedents'].apply(len)
strong_rules['rule'] = strong_rules.apply(
    lambda r: ', '.join(sorted(r['antecedents'])) + ' → ' +
              ', '.join(sorted(r['consequents'])), axis=1
)
strong_rules = strong_rules.sort_values('lift', ascending=False)

print(f"\\nStrong rules (conf≥0.50, lift≥2.0, supp≥0.01): {len(strong_rules)}")
print("\\nTop 20 rules by lift:")
print(strong_rules[['rule', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']].head(20).to_string())

)

Cell 6 — Targeted Rule Search + Business Interpretation

# --- What leads customers to buy whole milk? ---
def rules_for_item(rules_df, item, role='consequent'):
    if role == 'consequent':
        mask = rules_df['consequents'].apply(lambda x: item in x)
    else:
        mask = rules_df['antecedents'].apply(lambda x: item in x)
    return rules_df[mask].sort_values('lift', ascending=False)

milk_rules = rules_for_item(rules, 'whole milk', role='consequent')
milk_rules['rule'] = milk_rules.apply(
    lambda r: ', '.join(sorted(r['antecedents'])) + ' → whole milk', axis=1
)

print("=== Top 10 rules predicting whole milk purchase ===")
print(milk_rules[['rule', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']].head(10).to_string())

# --- Mutual strongest rules (both directions high lift) ---
print("\\n=== Top overall rules by lift ===")
print(strong_rules[['rule', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']].head(10).to_string())

# --- Business interpretation of top rule ---
top_rule = strong_rules.iloc[0]
ant = ', '.join(sorted(top_rule['antecedents']))
cons = ', '.join(sorted(top_rule['consequents']))
print(f"\\n=== Business Interpretation of Top Rule ===")
print(f"Rule:       {ant} → {cons}")
print(f"Support:    {top_rule['support']:.4f}")
print(f"Confidence: {top_rule['confidence']:.4f}")
print(f"Lift:       {top_rule['lift']:.4f}")
print(f"\\nIn plain language:")
print(f"  → {top_rule['support']:.1%} of all grocery baskets contain both '{ant}' and '{cons}'.")
print(f"  → Customers who buy '{ant}' also buy '{cons}' {top_rule['confidence']:.1%} of the time.")
print(f"  → That's {top_rule['lift']:.2f}x more likely than a random basket containing '{cons}'.")
print(f"\\nBusiness action: Place '{cons}' near '{ant}' in the store,")
print(f"or offer a bundle discount on these items together.")
Checklist before submitting Lab 7:
  • ✓ TransactionEncoder used to build one-hot matrix (not manual dummy variables)
  • ✓ fpgrowth used (not apriori) for speed
  • ✓ All three metrics — support, confidence, lift — reported for each rule
  • ✓ Rules filtered by all three metrics, not just one
  • ✓ Rule space scatter plot included
  • ✓ Top rules interpreted in business plain language
  • ✓ No causal language used (avoid "causes," "leads to" — use "associated with," "predicts")
  • ✓ Both FP-Growth result counts and rule count reported in write-up

Common Lab Mistakes to Avoid

  • Skipping TransactionEncoder: Manually looping to create dummy variables is error-prone. Use TransactionEncoder — it handles multi-item baskets and ordering correctly.
  • Using apriori on 10K+ row data: It will run, but slowly. Use fpgrowth.
  • Not setting use_colnames=True: Output shows integer indices instead of product names — unreadable.
  • Reporting only confidence: Always pair with lift. A "high confidence" rule with lift ≈ 1 is useless.
  • Treating rules as causal: Never write "buying diapers causes beer purchase." Write "diapers and beer are frequently co-purchased."
  • Not checking for NaN in lift: If a consequent has 100% support (appears in every transaction), you'll get lift = confidence/1 = confidence (fine), but items that never appear alone can cause NaN conviction values. Filter with rules.dropna() if needed.
