9.1 SQL from Zero SQL

SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to relational databases. Every serious data role uses it. When you have a 10-million-row table in a database, you don't load it into pandas first — you query it with SQL, filter it down to what you need, and bring the result into Python. At Southern Star, pipeline meter readings, maintenance work orders, and safety incident records all live in databases you'll query with SQL.

Database Concepts First

A relational database stores data in tables. Each table is a named grid of rows and columns — exactly like a DataFrame, but stored on disk and queryable by multiple users simultaneously.

ConceptDefinitionPipeline Example
TableA named set of rows with a fixed schemapipeline_segments, maintenance_orders, meter_readings
RowOne record — one entity or eventOne maintenance work order
ColumnOne attribute, same type for every rowsegment_id, flow_rate_mcf, reading_date
Primary KeyA column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each roworder_id in maintenance_orders
Foreign KeyA column in one table that references the primary key of another table — creates the relationshipsegment_id in meter_readings references segment_id in pipeline_segments
Southern Star's Enterprise Excellence team likely works with tables like: pipeline segments by region, daily/hourly flow meter readings, maintenance work orders, safety incident logs, compression station performance metrics, and customer delivery records. Every time you answer a business question like "which segments had flow below contract minimum last quarter," you're writing SQL.

The Sample Schema We'll Use

-- Three tables used in all examples below

pipeline_segments
  segment_id    INT PRIMARY KEY     -- unique ID per segment
  segment_name  VARCHAR             -- e.g., "Line 300 — Owensboro N"
  region        VARCHAR             -- 'North', 'South', 'East', 'West'
  length_miles  DECIMAL
  diameter_in   DECIMAL             -- pipe diameter in inches
  install_year  INT

meter_readings
  reading_id    INT PRIMARY KEY
  segment_id    INT FOREIGN KEY → pipeline_segments.segment_id
  reading_date  DATE
  flow_mcf      DECIMAL             -- flow in thousand cubic feet
  pressure_psi  DECIMAL
  status        VARCHAR             -- 'Normal', 'Alert', 'Critical'

maintenance_orders
  order_id      INT PRIMARY KEY
  segment_id    INT FOREIGN KEY → pipeline_segments.segment_id
  order_date    DATE
  order_type    VARCHAR             -- 'Inspection', 'Repair', 'Replacement'
  cost_usd      DECIMAL
  completed     BOOLEAN             -- TRUE/FALSE
  technician    VARCHAR

9.1a SELECT — Retrieving Data

Basic SELECT Structure

SELECT   column1, column2, ...       -- which columns to return (* = all)
FROM     table_name                  -- which table
WHERE    condition                   -- filter rows (optional)
ORDER BY column ASC|DESC            -- sort results (optional)
LIMIT    n;                         -- return only first n rows (optional)

Example 1 — All segments in the North region

SELECT  segment_id,
        segment_name,
        length_miles,
        diameter_in
FROM    pipeline_segments
WHERE   region = 'North'
ORDER BY length_miles DESC;

Example 2 — Meter readings in alert or critical status this year, most recent first

SELECT  reading_id,
        segment_id,
        reading_date,
        flow_mcf,
        pressure_psi,
        status
FROM    meter_readings
WHERE   status IN ('Alert', 'Critical')
  AND   reading_date >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY reading_date DESC
LIMIT   50;

Example 3 — Segments installed before 1990 (aging infrastructure flag)

SELECT  segment_name,
        region,
        install_year,
        length_miles,
        2026 - install_year AS age_years    -- calculated column with alias
FROM    pipeline_segments
WHERE   install_year < 1990
ORDER BY install_year ASC;

WHERE Operators Quick Reference

OperatorMeaningExample
=Equalsregion = 'North'
<> or !=Not equalsstatus <> 'Normal'
> < >= <=Comparisonsflow_mcf >= 1000
IN (...)Matches any value in listorder_type IN ('Repair','Replacement')
BETWEEN a AND bInclusive rangeinstall_year BETWEEN 1980 AND 1999
LIKE 'pattern'Pattern match (% = wildcard)segment_name LIKE 'Line 3%'
IS NULLMissing valuecost_usd IS NULL
AND / OR / NOTCombine conditionsregion = 'North' AND diameter_in > 20

9.1b JOINs — Combining Tables

A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a matching column (usually a primary key / foreign key pair). This is the most important concept in SQL for real-world work — data is almost never in one table.

INNER JOIN — Only Rows That Match in Both Tables

Returns rows where the join condition is true in BOTH tables. Rows without a match in the other table are excluded.

SELECT  ps.segment_name,
        ps.region,
        mr.reading_date,
        mr.flow_mcf,
        mr.pressure_psi,
        mr.status
FROM    meter_readings  AS mr
INNER JOIN pipeline_segments AS ps
    ON mr.segment_id = ps.segment_id
WHERE  mr.status = 'Critical'
ORDER BY mr.reading_date DESC;
Table aliases: meter_readings AS mr creates a short alias mr. Then mr.reading_date unambiguously refers to the reading_date column of meter_readings. Required when two tables have columns with the same name. Use them always — it makes queries readable.

LEFT JOIN — All Rows from Left Table, Matched Rows from Right

Returns ALL rows from the left table. Rows in the left table with no match in the right table still appear — they just get NULL for every right-table column. Use LEFT JOIN when you want to find "segments that have NO maintenance orders" or "customers with no readings this month."

-- Find all pipeline segments, with their most recent maintenance if any exists
-- Segments with NO maintenance orders will appear with NULL in order columns

SELECT  ps.segment_name,
        ps.region,
        ps.install_year,
        mo.order_date,
        mo.order_type,
        mo.cost_usd
FROM    pipeline_segments AS ps
LEFT JOIN maintenance_orders AS mo
    ON ps.segment_id = mo.segment_id
WHERE   mo.order_id IS NULL    -- keeps ONLY segments with no maintenance ever
ORDER BY ps.install_year ASC;

Three-Table JOIN

-- For each critical reading: segment name + most recent maintenance type
SELECT  ps.segment_name,
        ps.region,
        mr.reading_date,
        mr.flow_mcf,
        mr.status,
        mo.order_type       AS last_maintenance_type,
        mo.order_date       AS last_maintenance_date
FROM    meter_readings      AS mr
INNER JOIN pipeline_segments AS ps  ON mr.segment_id = ps.segment_id
LEFT JOIN  maintenance_orders AS mo ON ps.segment_id = mo.segment_id
WHERE   mr.status = 'Critical'
ORDER BY mr.reading_date DESC;
INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN: INNER removes non-matching rows from BOTH sides. LEFT keeps ALL rows from the left table regardless of whether they match. If you need "all segments even if no readings," put pipeline_segments on the left side of a LEFT JOIN. If you accidentally use INNER JOIN, segments with no readings silently disappear from your results — a common data-quality mistake.

9.1c GROUP BY and HAVING — Aggregating Data

GROUP BY collapses multiple rows into summary rows — one row per group. It always works with an aggregate function: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.

Basic GROUP BY

-- Total maintenance cost per region
SELECT  ps.region,
        COUNT(mo.order_id)              AS total_orders,
        SUM(mo.cost_usd)                AS total_cost,
        AVG(mo.cost_usd)                AS avg_cost_per_order,
        MIN(mo.order_date)              AS first_order,
        MAX(mo.order_date)              AS most_recent_order
FROM    maintenance_orders  AS mo
INNER JOIN pipeline_segments AS ps
    ON mo.segment_id = ps.segment_id
GROUP BY ps.region
ORDER BY total_cost DESC;

COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)

  • COUNT(*) — counts all rows, including those with NULLs
  • COUNT(column) — counts rows where that column is NOT NULL
  • COUNT(DISTINCT column) — counts distinct non-null values
-- How many distinct segments had a Critical reading in 2026?
SELECT  COUNT(DISTINCT segment_id) AS segments_with_critical_reading
FROM    meter_readings
WHERE   status = 'Critical'
  AND   reading_date >= '2026-01-01';

HAVING — Filtering After Grouping

WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping. HAVING filters aggregated groups AFTER grouping. You cannot use an aggregate function (SUM, COUNT, AVG) in a WHERE clause — that's what HAVING is for.

-- Which segments had total maintenance cost > $50,000 in 2026?
SELECT  ps.segment_name,
        ps.region,
        COUNT(mo.order_id)   AS order_count,
        SUM(mo.cost_usd)     AS total_cost_2026
FROM    maintenance_orders  AS mo
INNER JOIN pipeline_segments AS ps
    ON mo.segment_id = ps.segment_id
WHERE   mo.order_date >= '2026-01-01'       -- filter rows BEFORE grouping
  AND   mo.completed = TRUE
GROUP BY ps.segment_name, ps.region
HAVING  SUM(mo.cost_usd) > 50000           -- filter groups AFTER grouping
ORDER BY total_cost_2026 DESC;

Query Execution Order

SQL processes clauses in this order — different from the order you write them:

① FROM / JOIN → ② WHERE → ③ GROUP BY → ④ HAVING → ⑤ SELECT → ⑥ ORDER BY → ⑦ LIMIT

This is why you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE — WHERE runs before SELECT. And why aggregates must go in HAVING — WHERE runs before GROUP BY.

9.1d Answering a Business Question — Full Query Walkthrough

Real interview question: "Using the data available, identify which pipeline regions have the highest rate of non-normal meter readings and what maintenance has been done there." Here's how you'd build that query step by step. 
-- Business question: Which regions have the worst meter reading health in 2026?
-- Show: region, total readings, % non-normal, total maintenance cost YTD

SELECT
    ps.region,
    COUNT(mr.reading_id)                        AS total_readings,
    SUM(CASE WHEN mr.status <> 'Normal'
             THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)             AS non_normal_readings,
    ROUND(
        100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN mr.status <> 'Normal'
                         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
        / COUNT(mr.reading_id), 2
    )                                               AS pct_non_normal,
    COALESCE(SUM(mo.cost_usd), 0)              AS maintenance_cost_ytd
FROM   meter_readings       AS mr
INNER JOIN pipeline_segments AS ps
    ON mr.segment_id = ps.segment_id
LEFT JOIN  maintenance_orders AS mo
    ON  ps.segment_id = mo.segment_id
    AND mo.order_date >= '2026-01-01'
WHERE  mr.reading_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY ps.region
HAVING   COUNT(mr.reading_id) > 0
ORDER BY pct_non_normal DESC;
New SQL used above:
CASE WHEN condition THEN value ELSE other_value END — SQL's if/else inside a SELECT. Used here to count rows meeting a condition.
ROUND(value, decimal_places) — round a number to N decimal places.
COALESCE(expr, fallback) — returns the first non-NULL value. Prevents NULL appearing in the output when no maintenance costs exist for a region.

9.2 Excel Job-Ready Toolkit Excel

Excel is universal in energy and utilities — operational reports, budget tracking, maintenance logs, stakeholder summaries. At Southern Star you'll likely use it to build quick-turnaround summaries and presentation-ready tables before moving to Power BI for dashboards.

9.2a Lookups — XLOOKUP and INDEX+MATCH

XLOOKUP (Modern — Use This)

XLOOKUP replaces VLOOKUP. It searches a range for a value and returns a corresponding result from another range. It searches in any direction (not just left-to-right), handles errors gracefully, and returns a range (not just one cell).

Syntax:
=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode])

Required:
  lookup_value   — the value you're looking up
  lookup_array   — the column to search in
  return_array   — the column to return from

Optional:
  if_not_found   — what to show if no match found (instead of #N/A)
  match_mode     — 0=exact match (default), -1=next smaller, 1=next larger
  search_mode    — 1=first to last (default), -1=last to first
Example — look up a segment's region from a reference table:
  Segment IDs are in column A of Sheet2 (A2:A100)
  Regions are in column B of Sheet2 (B2:B100)
  You want the region for segment_id in cell B2 of Sheet1:

=XLOOKUP(B2, Sheet2!A2:A100, Sheet2!B2:B100, "Not Found")

Returns the region if segment_id is found; "Not Found" if not.
No need to know which column number — you reference the column directly.

XLOOKUP for Multiple Columns at Once

=XLOOKUP(B2, Sheet2!A2:A100, Sheet2!B2:D100)
-- Returns THREE columns (B, C, D) for the matching row — one formula, three results.

INDEX + MATCH (Classic — Know It, Use XLOOKUP in Practice)

INDEX returns a value from a range at a given row/column position. MATCH finds the position of a value in a range. Combined, they replicate XLOOKUP and work in older Excel versions.

INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, 0))
  -- The 0 in MATCH means exact match

Example:
=INDEX(Sheet2!B2:B100, MATCH(B2, Sheet2!A2:A100, 0))
-- Same result as the XLOOKUP example above
Interview answer: "I use XLOOKUP by default because it's more readable, handles left-side lookups without workarounds, and returns an array of columns in one formula. I know INDEX+MATCH and use it when working in an environment where XLOOKUP isn't available (Excel 2016 or older) or when I need a 2D lookup (INDEX with two MATCH functions — one for row, one for column)."

9.2b SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS and Nested IF

SUMIFS — Sum with Multiple Conditions

Syntax:
=SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...)

Example — Total maintenance cost for completed Repair orders in the North region:
=SUMIFS(D2:D500,       -- sum this column (cost_usd)
        C2:C500, "Repair",   -- where order_type = "Repair"
        E2:E500, "North",    -- AND region = "North"
        F2:F500, TRUE)       -- AND completed = TRUE

COUNTIFS — Count with Multiple Conditions

=COUNTIFS(C2:C500, "Alert",    -- count rows where status = "Alert"
           B2:B500, ">=" & DATE(2026,1,1))  -- AND reading_date >= Jan 1 2026
-- Note: use & to concatenate the operator with a cell reference or function

AVERAGEIFS — Average with Multiple Conditions

=AVERAGEIFS(D2:D500,            -- average this column (flow_mcf)
            E2:E500, "South",   -- where region = "South"
            F2:F500, "Normal")  -- AND status = "Normal"

Nested IF with AND / OR

-- Categorize a reading as Red/Yellow/Green based on status and flow
=IF(C2="Critical", "Red",
  IF(AND(C2="Alert", D2<500), "Red",
    IF(C2="Alert", "Yellow",
      "Green")))

-- Using OR to combine conditions
=IF(OR(C2="Critical", C2="Alert"), "Needs Review", "OK")

-- IF with AND:
=IF(AND(C2="Normal", D2>1000), "High Normal Flow", "Standard")
Nested IF depth: Excel allows up to 64 nested IFs, but anything beyond 3 levels becomes hard to maintain. Use IFS() (Excel 2019+) for cleaner multi-condition logic: =IFS(C2="Critical","Red", C2="Alert","Yellow", TRUE,"Green"). The TRUE at the end acts as the "else" fallback.

9.2c Text Functions

FunctionWhat it doesExampleResult
TRIM(text)Removes leading, trailing, and extra internal spaces=TRIM(" Line 300 ")"Line 300"
LEFT(text, n)First n characters=LEFT("Line 300",4)"Line"
RIGHT(text, n)Last n characters=RIGHT("2026-07-15",4)"2026" — wait, it's the rightmost 4 chars → "7-15"... actually "7-15" is 4 chars from right. For year use LEFT.
MID(text, start, n)n characters starting at position start=MID("2026-07-15",6,2)"07" (month)
LEN(text)Number of characters=LEN("Line 300")8
UPPER/LOWER/PROPERChange case=PROPER("north region")"North Region"
CONCATENATE / &Join strings=A2&" - "&B2"S101 - North"
SUBSTITUTE(text,old,new)Replace text=SUBSTITUTE(A2,"Line ","L-")"L-300"
FIND(find_text, within)Position of a string (case-sensitive, errors on miss)=FIND("-","2026-07-15")5
TEXTBEFORE/TEXTAFTERExtract before/after a delimiter (Excel 365)=TEXTBEFORE("Line 300 — North"," — ")"Line 300"
 
-- Practical: Extract year and month from a date column in text format "2026-07-15"
Year:  =LEFT(A2, 4)                     → "2026"
Month: =MID(A2, 6, 2)                   → "07"
Day:   =RIGHT(A2, 2)                    → "15"

-- Or if the column is a real Excel date (a number), use:
Year:  =YEAR(A2)
Month: =MONTH(A2)
Day:   =DAY(A2)

Remove Duplicates and Text to Columns

Remove Duplicates:
  Data tab → Data Tools group → Remove Duplicates
  Choose which columns define "duplicate" — often you want to remove rows
  where ALL columns match, not just one.

Text to Columns:
  Select the column → Data tab → Text to Columns
  Choose Delimited (comma, tab, pipe, custom character)
  or Fixed Width (characters at set positions)
  Useful when you import a CSV that all loaded into one column, or
  when a "Name, City" column needs to be split.

9.2d PivotTables

PivotTables summarize a data table interactively — drag fields to rows, columns, values, and filters without writing any formulas. For a 50,000-row maintenance log, a PivotTable lets you see "total cost by region by order type" in 10 seconds.

Creating a PivotTable:
1. Click anywhere inside your data table
2. Insert tab → PivotTable → New Worksheet
3. The PivotTable field list appears on the right

PivotTable field zones:
  FILTERS   — adds a dropdown filter above the table (e.g., filter to one year)
  COLUMNS   — creates column headers (e.g., order_type across the top)
  ROWS      — creates row labels (e.g., region down the left side)
  VALUES    — the numbers inside the table (e.g., Sum of cost_usd)

Example setup for maintenance analysis:
  ROWS:    region
  COLUMNS: order_type   (Inspection | Repair | Replacement)
  VALUES:  Sum of cost_usd
  FILTERS: year (from a year column you created from order_date)

Result: a grid showing total cost by region and order type.
Key PivotTable options:
  Right-click on a value → Summarize Values By → switch between Sum/Count/Avg/Min/Max
  Right-click on a row label → Group → group dates by Month/Quarter/Year automatically
  Insert tab → Slicer → adds a visual click-to-filter button panel
  Right-click on PivotTable → Refresh → updates when source data changes
  PivotChart: Insert tab → PivotChart → creates a chart tied to the PivotTable

9.2e Building a Clean, Presentation-Ready Chart

Steps to a clean chart:
1. Select the data range (include headers)
2. Insert tab → Charts → choose type (Bar, Column, Line, Scatter)
3. Click the chart → Chart Design tab → remove gridlines, border
4. Click chart title → type a descriptive title ("Q3 2026 Maintenance Cost by Region")
5. Click axis labels → format font size to match slide/report body text
6. Right-click data series → Format Data Series → clean up colors
   (use your company's brand colors or a 2–3 color palette — avoid rainbow)
7. Remove the legend if you have only one series
8. Add data labels if the chart will be printed or low-resolution

Common presentation mistakes:
  ❌ 3D charts — distort proportions, never use
  ❌ Too many colors — pick 1 primary color, 1 highlight color
  ❌ Cluttered gridlines — remove or make very light gray
  ❌ No axis labels — always label what the axis represents and units
  ❌ Default "Chart Title" text left in — always replace it

9.3 Power BI Fundamentals Power BI

Power BI is Microsoft's business intelligence platform. You build a report once, connect it to live data, and everyone in the organization can view an always-current dashboard in their browser. It's explicitly named in the Southern Star posting — "designing and developing a data service project using tools like Power BI."

Power BI Desktop

Free download (Windows). Where you build reports. Connect to data, model relationships, create visuals, write DAX measures. Save as .pbix file.

Power BI Service

Browser-based (app.powerbi.com). Where you publish and share reports. Set up auto-refresh schedules. Create dashboards by pinning visuals from multiple reports.

9.3a Import Data and Build a Model

Importing data into Power BI Desktop:
  Home → Get Data → choose source:
    Excel Workbook (.xlsx)
    Text/CSV (.csv)
    SQL Server (enter server name + database)
    SharePoint folder
    Web (URL to a table or API)

After connecting → Navigator window shows all sheets/tables/queries
Check "Transform Data" to open Power Query Editor for cleaning before loading.

Power Query Editor (data cleaning UI):
  Remove columns: right-click column header → Remove
  Rename columns: double-click column header
  Filter rows: click dropdown arrow on column header
  Change data type: click the type icon left of column name
  Split column: Transform → Split Column → By Delimiter
  Replace values: Transform → Replace Values
  When done: Home → Close & Apply → loads data into Power BI
Building relationships (Model view):
  Click the Model icon (3-table diagram) in the left sidebar
  Power BI auto-detects relationships based on matching column names
  To create manually: drag a column from one table to the matching column in another

  Relationship properties:
    Cardinality: One-to-Many (most common), Many-to-Many, One-to-One
    Cross-filter direction: Single (default) or Both

  Example:
    pipeline_segments[segment_id] → meter_readings[segment_id]   (1:Many)
    pipeline_segments[segment_id] → maintenance_orders[segment_id] (1:Many)

9.3b Visuals and Slicers

Building a visual:
1. Click in the canvas (blank area) to deselect
2. In Visualizations pane → click the visual type (bar chart icon, line chart, etc.)
3. In Fields pane → drag fields into the visual's wells:
   Bar chart wells:  Axis (category), Values (measure), Legend (color by)
   Line chart wells: X-axis (time/date), Y-axis (measure), Legend
   Card visual:      Fields (one measure — shows a single big number)
   Table visual:     Columns (any fields)

4. With visual selected → Format visual (paintbrush icon in Visualizations pane)
   to change colors, labels, borders, titles

Common visuals for an operations dashboard:
  Card:            Total pipeline miles, Total maintenance cost YTD
  Bar/column:      Cost by region, Order count by order type
  Line chart:      Daily flow_mcf over time, Pressure trend
  Map:             If you have lat/lon or region boundaries
  Table/Matrix:    Detailed drill-down data
Adding a Slicer:
1. Visualizations pane → click the Slicer icon (funnel/filter shape)
2. Drag the field you want to filter by into the slicer's Field well
   (e.g., drag "region" to create a region filter)
3. Clicking a region in the slicer now filters ALL visuals on the page

Slicer types (Format visual → Slicer settings → Style):
  List:       checkboxes for each value
  Dropdown:   compact dropdown selector
  Between:    for numeric or date ranges (e.g., date range picker)
  Tile:       large clickable buttons

9.3c Basic DAX Measures

DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is Power BI's formula language for creating calculated measures. A measure is a dynamic calculation — it recalculates based on whatever filters, slicers, and visual context is currently applied. It's column formulas on steroids.

Creating a measure:
  Home tab → New Measure   (or right-click a table in Fields pane → New Measure)
  Type the DAX formula → press Enter

Basic DAX functions:
-------------------

SUM:
  Total Cost = SUM(maintenance_orders[cost_usd])

COUNT:
  Order Count = COUNT(maintenance_orders[order_id])

DISTINCTCOUNT:
  Unique Segments = DISTINCTCOUNT(meter_readings[segment_id])

AVERAGE:
  Avg Flow = AVERAGE(meter_readings[flow_mcf])

DIVIDE (safe division — returns alternate value instead of error on division by zero):
  Avg Cost per Order = DIVIDE([Total Cost], [Order Count], 0)

CALCULATE (the most important DAX function — changes the filter context):
  Critical Readings = CALCULATE(
      COUNT(meter_readings[reading_id]),
      meter_readings[status] = "Critical"
  )

  North Maintenance Cost = CALCULATE(
      [Total Cost],
      pipeline_segments[region] = "North"
  )

RELATED (look up a value from a related table — like XLOOKUP inside DAX):
  Region = RELATED(pipeline_segments[region])
  -- Use in a calculated column in meter_readings to bring in the region from pipeline_segments

IF:
  Status Flag = IF([Avg Flow] < 500, "Low Flow", "Normal")
Calculated column vs. measure:
  Calculated column: computed once per row, stored in the table
    → Use for row-level attributes: "age_years = 2026 - [install_year]"
    → Right-click table in Fields → New Column

  Measure: computed dynamically based on current filter context, never stored
    → Use for aggregates: Total Cost, Avg Flow, Order Count
    → Right-click table in Fields → New Measure
    → Always better for aggregations — uses less memory
Publishing to Power BI Service:
  File → Publish → Publish to Power BI → select your workspace
  Open app.powerbi.com → find your report under "My workspace"
  Schedule refresh (requires a gateway for on-premises data sources):
    Dataset settings → Scheduled refresh → set frequency
A realistic first Power BI project at Southern Star: Import a CSV or SQL query result of maintenance orders → build a model connecting it to a segment reference table → create a one-page dashboard with: (1) a card showing total YTD cost, (2) a bar chart of cost by region, (3) a line chart of monthly order counts, (4) a region slicer. That's the full Power BI skill loop in one deliverable.

9.4 Tableau Fundamentals Tableau

Tableau is a visual analytics tool known for its drag-and-drop exploration interface. Southern Star's responsibilities section lists it alongside SQL, Python, and Excel. The core concepts are fast to learn if you understand data already.

Connecting to a Data Source

Open Tableau Desktop (or Tableau Public — free version)
Left panel → Connect →
  To a File:    Excel, Text (CSV), JSON, Spatial File
  To a Server:  SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, etc.

After connecting:
  The Data Source page shows your table(s)
  Drag tables into the canvas to join them
  Tableau auto-detects join keys — verify them before proceeding
  Click the join icon to change join type (inner, left, right, full)
  Click "Sheet 1" at the bottom to go to the workspace

Dimensions vs. Measures — The Most Important Tableau Concept

Every field in Tableau is classified as either a Dimension or a Measure. This is fundamental — mixing them up leads to wrong chart types and broken aggregations.

DimensionMeasure
What it isCategorical or qualitative field — describes what something isNumeric field — something you calculate or aggregate
Examplesregion, segment_name, order_type, status, technicianflow_mcf, cost_usd, length_miles, pressure_psi
What Tableau does with itGroups data, creates headers, colors categoriesAggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT) and plots on axes
Color of the pillBlueGreen
Default placementRows / Columns for groupingRows / Columns for size/length of bars/lines
Tableau interview question: "What's the difference between a dimension and a measure?" A dimension is categorical — it defines the groups (region, order type). A measure is quantitative — it's the value you aggregate across those groups (total cost, average flow). Putting a measure on the Color shelf gives a continuous color scale; putting a dimension gives discrete colors. Getting this wrong creates charts that don't make sense.

Building a Basic Bar Chart

Goal: Total maintenance cost by region (bar chart)

1. In Sheets view, left panel shows fields:
   Dimensions section: region, segment_name, order_type, ...
   Measures section: cost_usd, flow_mcf, ...

2. Drag "region" to the Rows shelf (creates row headers)
3. Drag "cost_usd" to the Columns shelf
   Tableau auto-aggregates → shows SUM(cost_usd) on the x-axis
4. You now have a horizontal bar chart
5. For vertical bars: drag region to Columns, cost_usd to Rows

6. Sort: click the sort icon in the toolbar (ascending/descending by measure)
7. Add data labels: Marks card → Label → check Show mark labels
8. Change color: Marks card → Color → Edit Colors → pick a palette

Building a Line Chart (Time Series)

Goal: Monthly total flow_mcf over time

1. Drag "reading_date" (a date field) to Columns
   Tableau auto-groups to YEAR by default — click the "+" to drill to Month
   Or right-click the date pill → choose Month / Quarter / Week / Day
2. Drag "flow_mcf" to Rows — Tableau shows SUM(flow_mcf) as the y-axis
3. Marks card shows Line by default for date x-axis
4. To color by region: drag "region" to the Color mark

Adding Filters

Method 1 — Quick filter shown to the user:
  Drag a field to the Filters shelf → configure (all, specific values, range, etc.)
  Right-click the filter pill → Show Filter → shows the filter as a UI control on the viz

Method 2 — Global filter affecting all sheets:
  Right-click the filter pill → Apply to Worksheets → All Using This Data Source

Building a Dashboard

1. Bottom of Tableau → click "New Dashboard" icon (or Dashboard menu → New Dashboard)
2. Left panel shows all your sheets (visualizations you built)
3. Drag sheets from the panel onto the dashboard canvas
4. Drag a Blank tile to create spacing between visuals
5. Resize sheets by dragging their borders

Adding interactivity:
  Click a sheet → click the funnel icon (Use as Filter) → clicking a bar in that
  chart now filters all other charts on the dashboard to that value

Dashboard sizing:
  Dashboard menu → Size → choose Fixed size (for consistent exports)
  or Automatic (adjusts to browser/screen)

Tableau vs. Power BI

TableauPower BI
StrengthVisual exploration, complex chart types, speed for ad-hoc analysisMicrosoft ecosystem integration, DAX power, affordable enterprise licensing
Formula languageTableau Calculated Fields (simpler syntax)DAX (more powerful but steeper learning curve)
SharingTableau Server / Tableau Online / Tableau PublicPower BI Service (browser-based)
CostMore expensive per seatIncluded in Microsoft 365 E3 and above
Southern Star likely usesMentioned in responsibilities sectionExplicitly in job overview + design section
Interview answer: "I've worked with both. Power BI integrates tightly with the Microsoft stack and DAX gives you a lot of analytical power, which I'd expect to use more heavily here given the Power BI focus in the job description. Tableau excels at fast visual exploration — I'd use it to quickly prototype a view before building it out in Power BI for production distribution."

9.5 R for Python Users R

The Southern Star posting lists R alongside Python. The qualifier in the qualifications section is "Experience or willingness to learn." You don't need to be an R expert — you need to be honest, confident, and demonstrate that you understand the ecosystem.

What R Is and When It's Used

R is a statistical computing language built for data analysis and visualization. It was designed by statisticians for statisticians — its core strengths are statistical modeling, hypothesis testing, and publication-quality visualizations. Python has largely caught up in most of these areas, which is why many teams use both or have migrated to Python-first workflows.

RPython
Primary domainStatistical analysis, academic research, bioinformaticsGeneral-purpose: ML, NLP, web, automation, data engineering
Visualizationggplot2 (grammar of graphics — very powerful)matplotlib, seaborn, plotly
Data manipulationdplyr + tidyr (tidyverse)pandas
Machine learningcaret, tidymodelsscikit-learn (larger ecosystem)
ReportingR Markdown, Quarto (document + code together)Jupyter Notebooks
Package ecosystemCRAN (~20K packages)PyPI (~500K packages)
Key advantageStatistical modeling depth, ggplot2 qualityML ecosystem, production deployment, broader industry adoption

Key R Packages to Know by Name

  • tidyverse — meta-package including ggplot2 (viz), dplyr (data manipulation), tidyr (reshaping), readr (CSV import), stringr (strings), forcats (factors)
  • ggplot2 — the gold standard for static statistical visualizations; uses a "grammar of graphics" (layers of aesthetics, geometries, scales)
  • dplyr — data manipulation with functions like filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by(), summarise() — these map almost directly to pandas operations
  • tidyr — reshape data: pivot_wider() / pivot_longer() (equivalent to pandas pivot_table / melt)
  • caret / tidymodels — machine learning workflows (train/test split, cross-validation, model training)

R ↔ Python Concept Mapping

# Python pandas             # R dplyr equivalent
df.head(5)                  head(df, 5)
df[df['col'] > 5]           filter(df, col > 5)
df[['a','b','c']]           select(df, a, b, c)
df.assign(new=df['a']*2)    mutate(df, new = a * 2)
df.groupby('col').mean()    df %>% group_by(col) %>% summarise(mean = mean(val))

# The pipe operator in R: %>% (or |> in modern R)
# Equivalent to Python method chaining: df.filter().groupby().agg()
# ggplot2 quick example (R) vs matplotlib (Python)

# R — ggplot2
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(df, aes(x = region, y = cost_usd, fill = order_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Maintenance Cost by Region", x = "Region", y = "Cost (USD)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Python — matplotlib/seaborn equivalent
import seaborn as sns
sns.barplot(data=df, x='region', y='cost_usd', hue='order_type')
plt.title("Maintenance Cost by Region")
Exact interview answer to "Do you know R?":

"I know Python as my primary analytics language — I've used it for data cleaning, regression modeling, clustering, and NLP in my analytics coursework. I haven't done a large project in R, but I understand the ecosystem: the tidyverse handles data manipulation similarly to pandas, ggplot2 is the go-to for statistical visualization, and the syntax is conceptually similar enough that I could pick it up quickly. If the role uses R heavily, I'm confident I could be productive within a few weeks."

This is honest, specific, and shows intellectual confidence without overclaiming.

9.6 Interview Prep — Southern Star Enterprise Excellence

Southern Star is a natural gas pipeline company founded in 1904, headquartered in Owensboro, KY. The Enterprise Excellence team drives operational improvement through data. This internship is specifically about building a "data service project" — not a vague analytics assignment, an actual deliverable they'll use. They mentioned AI-assisted analytics, which aligns directly with what you've been building.

Likely Technical Interview Questions

Walk me through how you would analyze a dataset to find operational inefficiencies.
"I'd start with EDA — checking for missing data, understanding distributions of key variables, and looking for outliers that might indicate data quality issues or genuine anomalies. Then I'd look at time trends: are costs increasing quarter over quarter? Are there regions or segment types that consistently underperform? I'd use groupby aggregations to surface those patterns, and if the data supports it, I'd build a regression to quantify which factors actually drive the variation versus which ones are just correlated with it."
Tell me about a time you used data to support a decision.
Use your AN306 Presentation 4 — group project applying NLP, clustering, and geospatial analysis to 2026 US job market data. Lead with the business question you answered, the method you used to answer it, and the specific insight that resulted. Keep it concrete: "We found that X% of data analyst postings in the Midwest required Power BI but only Y% required Tableau — which changed how we framed our skills section."
What's the difference between a JOIN and a subquery in SQL?
"A JOIN combines rows from two tables horizontally — you get columns from both tables side by side based on a matching condition. A subquery is a query nested inside another query — the inner query runs first, and its result is used as a table or condition in the outer query. For most use cases, JOINs are preferred because they're more readable and databases optimize them better. Subqueries are useful when you need to filter using an aggregated result — for example, 'show segments where cost is above the average,' where you need the average first."
How would you build a dashboard to track pipeline maintenance performance?
"I'd start by talking to the stakeholders about what decisions the dashboard needs to support — before touching any tool. For maintenance performance, that probably means: cost trending, order completion rates, segments with the most issues, and technician workload. I'd then identify the data sources — likely a maintenance work order database — write SQL to pull the aggregated data I need, and build the visuals in Power BI: a card for total YTD cost, a bar chart by region, a line chart of monthly order volume, and a table for drill-down. I'd add slicers for region and order type so users can self-serve the view they need."
How do you handle missing data?
"It depends on the nature of the missing data and how it's missing. First I figure out why it's missing — is it random, or is there a pattern? If pressure readings are missing for certain segments at certain times, that might mean the sensor went offline, which is itself an insight. For numerical columns I might fill with the median if the missingness is random and low-volume. For categorical columns I'll flag as 'Unknown' rather than drop, unless the missingness is too high to be useful. I always document what I did and why, so anyone auditing the analysis understands the choices."

Questions to Ask Southern Star

  • "What does the actual data service project typically look like — do interns scope it themselves, or is there a defined problem statement at the start of the summer?"
  • "Which of the tools — Power BI, SQL, Python — does the Enterprise Excellence team use most day-to-day?"
  • "How does the team currently use AI or automation in its analytics workflows, and where are the biggest opportunities you haven't been able to get to yet?"
  • "What does a successful intern look like at the end of 12 weeks — is there a presentation, a deliverable handed off, something that stays in production?"
  • "What's the biggest data challenge the operations team is dealing with right now?"
Your edge in this interview: Most internship candidates can describe SQL and Excel. You can describe building an end-to-end analytics pipeline — NLP on job postings, clustering, regression, time-series forecasting — and explain why you made each modeling decision. The Southern Star post mentions "AI-enabled process improvement" and "AI-assisted analytics tools." That's your differentiator. Connect your Greenbabe AI pipeline and your AN306 ML work directly to their language about applying AI to business problems.

Part 1: Foundations Part 4: Regression Part 12: Model Selection & RF Part 13: Stats Foundations

Part 10a — How Neural Networks Learn

From "what is a slope?" to backpropagation — the full story of how a model teaches itself, starting from zero

10a.1 How Does Learning Actually Happen?

Every model in this course — regression, random forests, clustering — has one thing in common: it adjusts itself until it gets better at a task. But how does it adjust? What does "getting better" actually mean in math?

This part answers that question completely. By the end, you'll understand exactly why derivatives and the chain rule are the engine inside every AI system — from a simple linear regression to GPT-4.

🎯 The Core Idea (before any math)

Imagine you're blindfolded on a hilly landscape and your goal is to reach the lowest valley. You can't see the whole landscape. But you can feel the ground under your feet — specifically, which direction it slopes downward. So you take a step downhill. Then another. Eventually you reach the bottom.

That's exactly what a neural network does. The "landscape" is the error on the training data. The network's weights (the numbers inside it) are its position on that landscape. Derivatives tell it which direction is "downhill."

Before we get to neural networks specifically, let's make sure the idea of "adjusting weights to minimize error" feels completely familiar — because you already saw it in Part 4.

10a.2 You Already Saw This: The OLS Bridge

Connects to Part 4

In Part 4, you learned that linear regression finds the best fit line by minimizing the sum of squared residuals (SSR). The line y = mx + b has two adjustable numbers: slope m and intercept b. OLS found the exact values of m and b that made SSR as small as possible.

How did OLS find those best values? By taking the derivative of SSR with respect to each parameter, setting it to zero, and solving. This is calculus optimization — minimize a function by finding where its slope is zero.

OLS uses one exact derivative calculation to find the minimum directly. This works because a straight line has a "bowl-shaped" error function with one clear bottom. Neural networks have millions of parameters and highly complex error landscapes — you can't solve for the exact minimum with one formula. Instead, you walk toward it using gradient descent.

So everything that follows is the same idea as OLS regression — just scaled up to millions of parameters and without an exact closed-form solution.

OLS (Linear Regression)

  • 2 parameters (slope, intercept)
  • Find minimum once using algebra
  • Exact answer, no iteration needed
  • Works because error surface = simple bowl

Neural Networks

  • Millions to billions of parameters
  • Can't solve algebraically
  • Walk toward minimum step by step
  • Error surface = bumpy landscape with many valleys

10a.3 Derivatives Without the Textbook

A derivative answers one question: "If I nudge this input slightly, how much does the output change?"

That's it. No limits, no epsilons, no formal definition needed. Just: input changes a tiny bit → how much does the output move?

🏔️ The Hill Analogy

You're standing on a hill. The hill's height at your position is the output. Your position is the input. The derivative at your current position is the slope of the ground directly under your feet — how steeply and in which direction the hill rises.

If the slope under you is +5 (the hill goes up steeply to your right), and you move one foot to the right, you go up about 5 feet. If the slope is −2, moving one foot to the right takes you down about 2 feet. The derivative is just that slope number.

A concrete example with real numbers

Suppose your loss function (the error your model makes) is:

Simple Loss Function Loss(w) = w² − 4w + 5

If the weight w is currently set to 3, the loss is: 3² − 4(3) + 5 = 9 − 12 + 5 = 2.

The derivative of this loss with respect to w is: d(Loss)/dw = 2w − 4.

At w = 3: derivative = 2(3) − 4 = +2. This means: if you increase w by 1, the loss increases by about 2. The hill is rising. So to decrease the loss, you should move in the opposite direction: decrease w.

The minimum of this loss is where the derivative = 0: 2w − 4 = 0 → w = 2. At w = 2: Loss = 4 − 8 + 5 = 1. That's the best possible value of w for this function.

Simple Example — Derivative as "which way to adjust":
Current weight w = 5. Loss = 5² − 4(5) + 5 = 10. Derivative = 2(5) − 4 = +6.
Since the derivative is positive, increasing w makes loss go UP. So decrease w.
New weight: w = 5 − 0.1 × 6 = 4.4. New loss = 4.4² − 4(4.4) + 5 = 19.36 − 17.6 + 5 = 6.76.
Loss went down from 10 to 6.76. We moved in the right direction!

Why this is called "the gradient"

When you have one parameter, the derivative is just a number (the slope). When you have millions of parameters, each one has its own derivative. The gradient is the collection of all those derivatives together — a list saying "here's which direction each parameter should move to decrease the loss."

Gradient = Direction of Steepest Uphill ∇Loss = [ ∂Loss/∂w₁ , ∂Loss/∂w₂ , ∂Loss/∂w₃ , ... ]

To decrease the loss, you move in the opposite direction of the gradient (downhill). That's gradient descent — descending the gradient.

10a.4 Gradient Descent: Rolling Downhill

The algorithm that makes neural networks learn is called gradient descent. Here's the full procedure:

1
Make a prediction with the current weights. (Forward pass)
2
Compute the loss — how wrong was the prediction? (e.g., Mean Squared Error)
3
Compute the gradient — the derivative of the loss with respect to each weight.
4
Update each weight by moving it a small step opposite the gradient direction.
5
Repeat for thousands to millions of steps until loss is minimized.

The "small step" size is controlled by the learning rate (usually written as α or η). Too big a step and you overshoot the valley; too small and training takes forever.

Weight Update Rule (the core equation of deep learning) wnew = wold − α × (∂Loss / ∂w)
Concrete update example:
Current weight: w = 3.0. Learning rate: α = 0.1. Gradient: ∂Loss/∂w = +2.0.
New weight: w = 3.0 − 0.1 × 2.0 = 3.0 − 0.2 = 2.8.
We nudged w slightly downhill. After thousands of these nudges, w eventually reaches the optimal value (2.0 in our earlier example).
The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase (uphill). Gradient descent means stepping in the opposite direction (downhill). This is why the update rule subtracts the gradient rather than adding it.

10a.5 The Problem With Many Layers

A single-layer model is straightforward — there's one set of weights directly connecting inputs to outputs. Computing the gradient is simple. But neural networks have many layers: each layer transforms the data and passes it to the next.

Why layers? Each layer learns a different level of abstraction. In an image-recognition network, early layers learn to detect edges. Middle layers learn shapes. Later layers learn faces or objects. This layered representation is what makes deep learning so powerful.

The problem: layer 1's weights don't directly touch the loss. They touch layer 2, which touches layer 3, which eventually produces the output that gets compared to the true label. So how do we know which direction to adjust layer 1's weights?

📡 The Signal Problem

Imagine a game of telephone. You (layer 1) whisper to your neighbor (layer 2), who whispers to their neighbor (layer 3), who finally speaks the answer aloud. If the final answer is wrong, who's responsible? By how much did you contribute to the error? The chain rule is exactly the math that traces responsibility backwards through the chain.

Let's make this concrete with a simple 2-layer network:

Input (x) → [Layer 1 weight: w₁] → Hidden value (h) → [Layer 2 weight: w₂] → Output (ŷ) → Loss

To update w₁, we need: how does the loss change when we change w₁?

w₁ affects h. h affects ŷ. ŷ affects Loss. So the total effect of w₁ on Loss goes through two steps. We need a way to chain those effects together. That's the chain rule.

10a.6 The Chain Rule: The Domino Effect

The chain rule is a simple idea from calculus: when two things are linked together, you multiply their individual rates of change to get the combined rate of change.

🁢 Domino Analogy

Pushing domino A knocks over domino B with 3× the force you applied. Domino B then knocks over domino C with 2× the force it received. So from your push on A to the effect on C, the total amplification is 3 × 2 = 6×. You multiply the individual rates through each link in the chain.

The Chain Rule If z depends on y, and y depends on x:
dz/dx = (dz/dy) × (dy/dx)

In plain words: "how much does z change when x changes" = "how much does z change when y changes" × "how much does y change when x changes."

Applied to our 2-layer network

Recall our network: x → w₁ → h → w₂ → ŷ → Loss.

To find how the Loss responds to a change in w₁:

Chain Rule Applied to Layers ∂Loss/∂w₁ = (∂Loss/∂ŷ) × (∂ŷ/∂h) × (∂h/∂w₁)

Each factor is the derivative of one step in the chain:

  • ∂Loss/∂ŷ — how does the loss change when the output changes? (easy to compute)
  • ∂ŷ/∂h — how does the output change when the hidden value changes? (layer 2's local derivative)
  • ∂h/∂w₁ — how does the hidden value change when w₁ changes? (layer 1's local derivative)
Worked example with real numbers:
Suppose: h = w₁ × x = 0.5 × 2 = 1.0. ŷ = w₂ × h = 3.0 × 1.0 = 3.0. True label y = 5. Loss = (ŷ − y)² = (3 − 5)² = 4.

Step 1: ∂Loss/∂ŷ = 2(ŷ − y) = 2(3 − 5) = −4
Step 2: ∂ŷ/∂h = w₂ = 3.0
Step 3: ∂h/∂w₁ = x = 2.0

Chain rule result: ∂Loss/∂w₁ = (−4) × 3.0 × 2.0 = −24

With learning rate α = 0.01: w₁ becomes 0.5 − 0.01 × (−24) = 0.5 + 0.24 = 0.74.
Since the gradient was negative (−24), the update increases w₁ — moving the prediction closer to 5.

The critical insight: each layer only needs to know its own local derivative. It receives a "blame signal" from the layer above, multiplies by its local derivative, and passes the result back to the layer below. This is exactly what backpropagation does.

10a.7 Backpropagation: Sending Blame Backwards

Backpropagation (or "backprop") is just the chain rule applied systematically through every layer of a neural network — from the output layer back to the input layer. It's the algorithm that computes all the gradients needed for gradient descent in one efficient pass.

The name comes from what it does: it propagates the error (the "blame" for getting the prediction wrong) backward through the network, computing each weight's contribution to the error along the way.

The two passes every training step takes

→
Forward Pass: Run the input through every layer from first to last. Compute the final prediction. Compute the loss. Save the intermediate values at each layer (you'll need them in the backward pass).
←
Backward Pass (Backprop): Start at the loss. Compute ∂Loss/∂output. Multiply by the last layer's local derivative to get the gradient for the last layer's weights. Pass the signal back one more layer. Repeat until you've computed gradients for every weight in the network.
Why is backprop efficient? Without backprop, you'd have to nudge each weight individually and re-run the forward pass to see how the loss changed — that's millions of forward passes for a large network. Backprop computes ALL gradients in a single backward pass by cleverly reusing intermediate derivatives. This is what made deep learning computationally feasible.

Visual walkthrough: 3-layer network

INPUT x
   ↓
[Layer 1]  weights W₁  →  hidden₁ = W₁ · x + b₁  →  activation₁
   ↓
[Layer 2]  weights W₂  →  hidden₂ = W₂ · a₁ + b₂  →  activation₂
   ↓
[Layer 3]  weights W₃  →  output  = W₃ · a₂ + b₃
   ↓
  Loss = MSE(output, true_label)

─── Forward: left to right ──────────────────────────────────────────────
─── Backward: right to left ─────────────────────────────────────────────

∂Loss/∂W₃ = ∂Loss/∂output × ∂output/∂W₃          ← easy, one step
∂Loss/∂W₂ = ∂Loss/∂output × ∂output/∂a₂ × ∂a₂/∂W₂  ← two steps (chain rule)
∂Loss/∂W₁ = (above) × ∂a₂/∂a₁ × ∂a₁/∂W₁          ← three steps (chain rule)
Activation functions — you'll notice the word "activation" above. Each layer applies a function like ReLU (max(0, x)) or sigmoid (1/(1+e⁻ˣ)) to its output before passing it to the next layer. These add nonlinearity (without them, stacking layers would just be one big linear regression). The chain rule still applies — you just include the derivative of the activation function as one more factor in the chain. For ReLU: derivative is 1 if input > 0, else 0.

10a.8 Watching It Learn in Python

Here's a minimal but complete neural network training loop in PyTorch — the library that handles backprop automatically with loss.backward():

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# A tiny neural network: 1 input → 4 hidden → 1 output
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(1, 4),   # Layer 1: 1 input → 4 hidden neurons
    nn.ReLU(),          # Activation: max(0, x)
    nn.Linear(4, 1)    # Layer 2: 4 hidden → 1 output
)

optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()

# Toy data: y = 2x + 1
X = torch.tensor([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0]])
y = torch.tensor([[3.0], [5.0], [7.0], [9.0]])

# Training loop
for epoch in range(1000):
    # 1. FORWARD PASS — compute predictions
    y_pred = model(X)

    # 2. COMPUTE LOSS
    loss = loss_fn(y_pred, y)

    # 3. BACKWARD PASS — compute all gradients via chain rule
    optimizer.zero_grad()   # clear old gradients first
    loss.backward()         # THIS IS BACKPROP — PyTorch handles all the chain rule math

    # 4. UPDATE WEIGHTS — gradient descent step
    optimizer.step()

    if epoch % 100 == 0:
        print(f"Epoch {epoch}: Loss = {loss.item():.4f}")

# Output (approximate):
Epoch 0:    Loss = 42.3851
Epoch 100:  Loss = 0.9412
Epoch 200:  Loss = 0.1823
Epoch 300:  Loss = 0.0407
Epoch 400:  Loss = 0.0094
Epoch 500:  Loss = 0.0022
Epoch 600:  Loss = 0.0005
Epoch 700:  Loss = 0.0001
Epoch 800:  Loss = 0.0000
Epoch 900:  Loss = 0.0000
What loss.backward() actually does: PyTorch tracks every operation your data goes through during the forward pass (this is called "building a computation graph"). When you call loss.backward(), it traverses that graph in reverse, applying the chain rule at each node to compute the gradient for every weight. All the derivative math from Section 10a.6 happens automatically in one line.

Stochastic vs. Batch gradient descent

In the example above, we computed the loss over ALL 4 training examples at once before updating weights. This is called batch gradient descent. For large datasets (millions of rows), this is too slow. Instead, training splits the data into mini-batches (typically 32–256 rows) and does one gradient descent step per batch. This is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and is what modern deep learning uses.

MethodUpdate frequencyGradient qualitySpeed
Batch GDOnce per full dataset passExact (but can get stuck)Slow for large data
Stochastic GD (SGD)Once per single exampleNoisy but fastFast but chaotic
Mini-batch SGDOnce per batch (32–256 rows)Good balanceStandard in practice

10a.9 Why GPUs Changed Everything

Backpropagation was theoretically understood by the 1970s and popularized by Rumelhart and Hinton in 1986. But neural networks were still toy-sized for another 25 years. What changed?

GPUs.

The core operation in a neural network is matrix multiplication: multiplying large rectangular arrays of numbers together. This is what computing W · x + b means — multiply a weight matrix by an input vector and add a bias vector. GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) were originally designed to render 3D graphics, which also requires massive parallel matrix operations. It turned out they were perfect for neural networks too.

CPU

  • 8–64 powerful cores
  • Runs tasks sequentially — fast for logic and branching
  • Matrix multiply: runs row by row
  • A 10,000×10,000 matrix multiply: minutes

GPU

  • Thousands of small cores (NVIDIA A100: 6,912 cores)
  • Runs thousands of operations in parallel
  • Matrix multiply: all rows simultaneously
  • Same 10,000×10,000 matrix multiply: seconds

In 2007, Nvidia released CUDA — a programming interface that let developers use GPUs for general computation (not just graphics). In 2012, three researchers at University of Toronto used GPUs to train AlexNet, an 8-layer convolutional neural network, on ImageNet (1.2 million images, 1,000 categories). AlexNet reduced the image classification error rate from 26% to 15% — a jump so large it shocked the field and launched the modern deep learning era.

The key insight from AlexNet (2012): The architecture wasn't revolutionary. What was revolutionary was that it was trained on GPUs, which made it possible to use 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons — 10× larger than anything before. Scale + GPUs + data (ImageNet) was the recipe that unlocked deep learning.

The same recipe — more parameters, more data, more GPU compute — is what explains the entire progression from AlexNet to GPT-4. Part 10b covers how that scaling produced language models.

10a.10 What You Now Know

The Complete Picture of Neural Network Learning
  1. A neural network is a function with millions of adjustable weights stacked in layers.
  2. Training = minimizing a loss function that measures how wrong the network's predictions are.
  3. Derivatives tell us which direction to adjust each weight to reduce the loss — the direction of "downhill."
  4. Gradient descent repeatedly takes small steps downhill (w = w − α × gradient) until the loss is minimized.
  5. The chain rule lets us compute the gradient for weights deep in the network by multiplying derivatives through the chain of layers.
  6. Backpropagation applies the chain rule efficiently — one backward pass computes all gradients in the network simultaneously.
  7. GPUs make this feasible at scale by computing thousands of matrix multiplications in parallel.

Every AI system you encounter — image classifiers, speech recognition, translation engines, and the LLMs you interact with daily — learns using exactly this mechanism. The math never changes. Only the scale does.

Where to go next: Part 10b uses everything you just learned as the foundation to explain what an LLM actually is — how "predict the next word, done at scale" produced something that can reason, write, and code.

From "predict the next word" to emergent intelligence — the complete story of how language models work

10b.1 The Problem Classical NLP Hit

Builds on Part 8b

In Part 8b, you learned the classical NLP toolkit: TF-IDF turns text into word-frequency vectors, topic modeling finds hidden themes, sentiment analysis classifies positive vs. negative. These tools are still useful — but they all share a fundamental limitation.

They treat words as independent symbols. "The river bank flooded" and "I visited the bank downtown" have the same word "bank" but completely different meanings. TF-IDF can't tell them apart. It just counts — it has no concept of context, word order, or meaning.

Language is fundamentally contextual. The same word means different things in different positions. Any system that ignores this will plateau quickly. The question researchers struggled with for decades: how do you build a model that understands context?

🎯 The Goal

Read this sentence: "The trophy doesn't fit in the suitcase because it's too big."

What is "it" referring to — the trophy or the suitcase? You immediately know it's the trophy. You figured this out by tracking what "it" refers to across the whole sentence, understanding the logical relationship of "fit in" and "too big." A classical bag-of-words model has no way to reason about this. The goal of LLMs is to build a system that can.

10b.2 Tokens: How Text Becomes Numbers

Before any math can happen, text must become numbers. The first step is tokenization — splitting text into small pieces called tokens, then mapping each token to an integer ID.

Tokens aren't simply words. They're sub-word units that balance vocabulary size with coverage. Common words get their own token ("the" → 262). Rare words get split ("unbelievable" → ["un", "believ", "able"] → [946, 7540, 540]). This lets a fixed vocabulary of ~50,000 tokens cover any text in English.

Tokenization in practice:
Sentence: "Hello, I'm learning about LLMs."
Tokens: ["Hello", ",", " I", "'m", " learning", " about", " LL", "Ms", "."]
Token IDs: [15339, 11, 314, 1101, 4673, 546, 27140, 44, 13]

Notice: "LLMs" gets split because it's uncommon. Spaces are part of the token (the " " before "learning"). Punctuation gets its own token. This granularity lets the model handle any text — including made-up words and code.

The model only ever sees these integer IDs. Everything that follows — embeddings, attention, predictions — operates on these numbers.

10b.3 Embeddings: Putting Words on a Map

Connects to Part 8b embeddings section

An integer ID like 15339 doesn't tell the model anything about what "Hello" means or how it relates to "Hi" or "Greetings." To give words meaning, each token ID gets converted to an embedding: a list of numbers (a vector) that places the word in a high-dimensional space where similar words land near each other.

🗺️ The Map Analogy

Imagine plotting words on a 2D map. Words with similar meanings cluster together. "King" and "Queen" land close to each other. "Dog" and "Cat" land close to each other but far from "King." "Paris" and "France" are close, just like "Tokyo" and "Japan."

An embedding is this same idea, but in 768 or 1024 or 4096 dimensions instead of 2. More dimensions = more nuance. The model can represent more complex relationships between words when it has more room to spread them out.

What makes embeddings remarkable: the relationships are learned from data, not hand-coded. After training on billions of sentences, the model figures out on its own that "King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen." These relationships emerge from pure co-occurrence patterns.

Key difference from classical NLP: TF-IDF vectors are sparse (mostly zeros, one entry per unique word in the vocabulary). Embeddings are dense (every dimension has a meaningful value). This density is what lets models capture subtle similarities. "Joyful" and "happy" have high cosine similarity in embedding space even though they're different words.

10b.4 The Core Task: Predict the Next Word

Here's the most surprising thing about LLMs: they're trained on one absurdly simple task.

The Core Training Task

Given all the words so far, predict the next one.

That's it. The training data is just text — Wikipedia, books, Reddit, GitHub, news articles, scientific papers. For each position in that text, the model sees all the previous words and must predict the next one. It's scored by how well it guesses (using a loss function called cross-entropy, minimized via backpropagation from Part 10a).

How the task creates a dataset automatically:
Take one sentence: "The cat sat on the mat."
This generates 5 training examples automatically:
→ Input: ["The"] → Predict: "cat"
→ Input: ["The", "cat"] → Predict: "sat"
→ Input: ["The", "cat", "sat"] → Predict: "on"
→ Input: ["The", "cat", "sat", "on"] → Predict: "the"
→ Input: ["The", "cat", "sat", "on", "the"] → Predict: "mat"

With trillions of tokens of text, you get trillions of training examples — all self-supervised, requiring no human labels.

The question then becomes: how do you build a model that can get good at this task? The model needs to understand context — "The cat sat on the ___" is easy. But "In quantum mechanics, the wave function represents the probability amplitude of a particle's state, and when observed, it ___" requires understanding a whole chain of technical concepts. The model needs to look back at every previous word and decide which ones matter for predicting the next.

This is exactly what the attention mechanism solves.

10b.5 Attention: Looking Around for Context

The word "attention" in this context means: when processing a word, how much should the model focus on each other word in the sequence?

👁️ The Reading Analogy

When you read "The bank near the river flooded," your brain pays extra attention to "river" when it processes "bank" — because "river" resolves the ambiguity. When you read "She deposited money at the bank," your brain pays attention to "deposited" and "money" instead. You automatically focus on the most relevant words based on the context.

Attention mechanisms give a neural network this same ability: for each word being processed, compute a score for how relevant every other word is, and use those scores to build a richer representation of the current word.

How attention actually computes these scores

For each token, the model creates three vectors from its embedding:

  • Query (Q) — "What information am I looking for?" (What does the current token need to understand?)
  • Key (K) — "What information do I offer?" (What does each other token represent?)
  • Value (V) — "What information will I actually give?" (The content that gets passed forward)

The attention score between two tokens is computed as the dot product of Q and K (then scaled and softmaxed). High dot product = high relevance. The model then takes a weighted sum of all Value vectors, where the weights are the attention scores.

Scaled Dot-Product Attention Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √dₖ) · V
Intuitive breakdown of the formula:
Q·Kᵀ — multiply every query against every key to get a score for every pair of tokens. A high score = "this token is relevant to me."
/ √dₖ — divide by the square root of the dimension size to keep scores from getting too large (which would cause the softmax to saturate).
softmax(…) — convert the scores into probabilities that sum to 1 (how much attention to pay to each token).
· V — take a weighted average of the value vectors using those probabilities. The result is a new representation of the current token, enriched with information from the most relevant context tokens.

Multi-head attention: looking from many angles

Instead of computing attention once, transformers run it multiple times in parallel with different learned Q/K/V weight matrices — these are called attention heads. Each head learns to attend to different types of relationships:

  • One head might track subject-verb agreement ("The cats are" vs "The cat is")
  • Another head might track pronoun-antecedent relationships ("She" refers back to "Maria")
  • Another might track positional proximity
  • Another might track semantic similarity

The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected back to the original dimension size. This lets the model simultaneously capture many different types of linguistic relationships.

10b.6 The Transformer Architecture

The transformer (introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need") is the architecture that all modern LLMs are built on. It solved the core problem of earlier RNN-based models: RNNs processed words one at a time sequentially, which was slow and lost long-range context. Transformers process all tokens simultaneously and can attend to any position directly.

A transformer block: the repeating unit

INPUT TOKENS (after embedding)
         ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          TRANSFORMER BLOCK (×N)          │
│                                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │   Multi-Head Self-Attention      │    │
│  │   (every token looks at every    │    │
│  │   other token, computes weights) │    │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘    │
│                  ↓ + residual connection  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │   Layer Normalization            │    │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘    │
│                  ↓                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │   Feed-Forward Network (FFN)     │    │
│  │   (two linear layers + ReLU)     │    │
│  │   Applied identically to each   │    │
│  │   token position                 │    │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘    │
│                  ↓ + residual connection  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │   Layer Normalization            │    │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘    │
└──────────────────┼──────────────────────┘
                   ↓ (repeat this block N times)
         OUTPUT REPRESENTATIONS
                   ↓
         Linear layer + Softmax
                   ↓
      PROBABILITY OVER NEXT TOKEN
GPT-4 stacks ~96 of these blocks. Each block refines the token representations: early blocks capture syntax and local patterns; later blocks capture high-level semantics and reasoning. The residual connections (the "+" arrows) ensure that information from earlier representations isn't lost as it passes through many layers — this is what allows very deep networks to train without gradients vanishing.

Positional encoding: telling the model where words are

Attention by itself is order-agnostic — "cat sat the mat on" and "the cat sat on the mat" would look the same to pure attention because all tokens attend to all others regardless of position. To fix this, transformers add a positional encoding to each embedding before the first transformer block — a vector that encodes each token's position in the sequence. This lets the model learn position-sensitive patterns like "subjects come before verbs."

How scale looks in practice

ModelYearParametersTransformer BlocksKey milestone
GPT-12018117M12Showed pre-train then fine-tune works
BERT2018340M24Bidirectional (reads left AND right)
GPT-220191.5B48"Too dangerous to release" (OpenAI)
GPT-32020175B96Few-shot learning, in-context examples
GPT-42023~1.8T*~96Multimodal, near-human performance on many benchmarks
Claude 3.52024UnknownUnknownTop reasoning, long context

*GPT-4 architecture is not publicly disclosed; estimates vary widely.

10b.7 Pre-Training vs Fine-Tuning

Training an LLM happens in two distinct phases:

1
Pre-training: Train on massive text from the internet (Common Crawl, Wikipedia, books, code, etc.). The only task: predict the next token. This takes weeks to months on thousands of GPUs and costs millions of dollars. At the end, the model has learned language, facts, reasoning patterns, and world knowledge — all embedded in its weights. But it doesn't know how to follow instructions — it will just keep generating text in the style of whatever it was trained on.
2
Fine-tuning: Take the pre-trained model and continue training it on a smaller, curated dataset of (prompt, desired_response) pairs. This teaches the model how to respond to instructions rather than just completing text. The model already knows everything from pre-training — fine-tuning just teaches it the format and style of being a helpful assistant.
Analogy for pre-training vs fine-tuning:
Pre-training = going to school for 12 years. You absorb enormous amounts of information — history, science, math, language, culture. You didn't learn any of it to become a customer service rep specifically.
Fine-tuning = a 3-week onboarding program at your first job. You already know how to read, write, reason, and communicate. The onboarding just teaches you this company's specific processes, tone, and what good responses look like here.

10b.8 Scale and Emergence: The Surprise

When researchers first scaled language models, they expected gradual, predictable improvement. What they got instead was something nobody fully anticipated: emergent capabilities.

At certain parameter thresholds, models suddenly gained abilities that smaller models had zero performance on — not gradually, but as sharp jumps. 3-digit arithmetic: flat near zero until ~100B parameters, then suddenly 80%+ accuracy. Multi-step reasoning: flat then jump. Code generation: flat then jump.

💡 Why This Is Surprising

Imagine you're inflating a balloon. For a long time, nothing happens visually — the rubber just stretches. Then at a certain size, it suddenly becomes round and completely changes shape. Scaling laws have a similar feel: you add parameters and data, the next-token prediction loss decreases gradually, but at some scale the model suddenly generalizes in entirely new ways.

Nobody programmed GPT-3 to do French translation. Nobody programmed it to solve SAT analogy questions. It learned these things as side effects of getting very good at next-token prediction on a diverse enough corpus.

The scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020)

Researchers at OpenAI discovered that model performance follows predictable power laws as you scale three things: number of parameters (N), amount of training data (D), and compute budget (C). These Chinchilla scaling laws (refined 2022) established that optimal training uses roughly equal "compute" on model size and data: a model trained on 70B tokens needs roughly 70B parameters for best efficiency.

Scale more of thisWhat happens to lossWall you hit
Parameters (N)Smooth decrease in lossNeed more data to match; memory cost
Training data (D)Smooth decrease in lossDiminishing returns; data quality matters
Compute (C)Smooth decrease in lossCost and time
Why this matters for you: The scaling laws explain why the AI field moved from "clever algorithms" to "just make it bigger." From 2020 to 2024, the dominant strategy in AI research was simply: more parameters + more data + more compute = better model. The algorithmic insights matter, but the scaling multiplies their effect.

10b.9 RLHF: Teaching Helpfulness

A pre-trained model fine-tuned on (prompt, response) pairs is better, but still unreliable. It might give technically correct but unhelpful answers, refuse reasonable requests, or be inconsistently formatted. The breakthrough that turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT was Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

The three-step RLHF process

1
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Human contractors write ideal (prompt, response) pairs. The model is fine-tuned on these examples. This gives it a starting point for following instructions.
2
Train a Reward Model: For the same prompt, the model generates multiple responses. Human raters rank them from best to worst. A separate neural network (the "reward model") is trained to predict these human preference rankings — it learns what humans consider a "good" response.
3
RL Fine-Tuning (PPO): The main model is then optimized using reinforcement learning to generate responses that the reward model rates highly. It's trained to "win" at the reward model's scoring, subject to a constraint that it can't drift too far from the SFT checkpoint (to prevent reward hacking).
Why RLHF was the key unlock:
Before RLHF: "What are some ways to improve my essay?" → model might just generate more essays.
After RLHF: "What are some ways to improve my essay?" → model gives a structured list of concrete editing suggestions.

The difference: the reward model learned that humans prefer responsive, helpful, clearly formatted answers over technically-associated-but-not-useful completions. RLHF is how the model learned what "being an assistant" looks like.
RLHF does NOT teach the model new factual knowledge. It teaches the model how to respond. All facts, reasoning patterns, and language understanding come from pre-training. RLHF is about style, format, safety, and helpfulness — not new knowledge.

10b.10 What an LLM Actually Is (and Isn't)

Now you have all the pieces. Here's the complete honest picture:

What an LLM Is

A very large neural network (transformer architecture, billions of parameters) trained on a massive text corpus to predict the next token. Through that training, it has implicitly learned language structure, world knowledge, reasoning patterns, and common sense — all encoded in its weights as statistical patterns. RLHF then shaped how it expresses those patterns in response to prompts.

Under the hood: it's matrix multiplications, attention score computations, and softmax operations — all learned by backpropagation on the cross-entropy loss of next-token prediction.

What LLMs are genuinely good at

  • Language fluency: Grammar, style, tone, structure — from billions of examples
  • Pattern completion: Code, formulas, templates — anywhere the next token follows a pattern
  • Knowledge recall: Facts encoded during pre-training (with training data cutoff)
  • Transformation tasks: Summarize, translate, classify, extract — these map input text to output text
  • In-context learning: Give it examples in the prompt and it adapts behavior without retraining
  • Reasoning (via chain-of-thought): When prompted to "think step by step," models significantly improve at multi-step problems

What LLMs are not (common misconceptions)

MisconceptionReality
"It understands what it's saying"It predicts statistically likely next tokens. Whether this constitutes "understanding" is an open philosophical question. Practically: it behaves as if it understands for most tasks, but breaks on edge cases in ways a human wouldn't.
"It knows everything"It knows what was in its training data, up to its training cutoff date. Post-cutoff events, private documents, real-time data: it doesn't have access unless given in the prompt or via tools.
"It retrieves the right answer"It generates the most statistically likely continuation — which is usually the right answer, but can confidently produce plausible-sounding wrong answers ("hallucinations").
"Bigger is always better"Past a certain size, training data quality and instruction tuning matter more than raw parameter count. A well-tuned 70B model often outperforms a poorly-tuned 400B one.
"It's doing something magical"It's doing math. Very large-scale math, but math — matrix multiplications, attention scores, softmax, cross-entropy loss, gradient descent. The "magic" is an emergent property of that math at scale.

The road from here

2017
Transformer architecture published
Replaced RNNs; enabled parallel processing of sequences
2018–2019
BERT, GPT-1, GPT-2 — pre-train then fine-tune era
Showed that one pre-trained model could be adapted to many tasks
2020
GPT-3 — in-context learning at scale
175B parameters; few-shot prompting without fine-tuning; first "it just works" moment
2022
InstructGPT / ChatGPT — RLHF unlocks helpfulness
The first model the general public could productively use; 100M users in 2 months
2023
GPT-4, Claude 2, Gemini — multimodal, long context
Can see images; 100K+ token context windows; near-expert performance on professional exams
2024
Reasoning models (o1, o3), agents, MCP
Models that "think before answering"; tool use; autonomous multi-step task completion
2025–now
Agentic AI — LLMs as orchestrators
LLMs calling tools, browsing the web, writing and running code, coordinating sub-agents — the system you're using right now
The circle is complete. You started this course with a table of numbers and learned how to describe it (Part 1), how to find patterns in it (Parts 2–9), and how that same underlying math — fit a function, minimize a loss, use derivatives to improve — scaled up to produce the AI systems reshaping every industry. The chain rule from Part 10a and the attention mechanism from Part 10b are both just elaborations of the core idea: adjust parameters iteratively to fit a function to data.

Part 13: Statistical Inference from the Ground Up

Everything your intro statistics course taught — variable types through two-sample hypothesis tests — built into the foundations that make machine learning interpretable.

Why Statistics Before Machine Learning?

Every machine learning algorithm you've learned — regression, random forest, clustering — is built on statistical foundations. When you see R² = 0.85, that's statistics. When a data scientist says "this feature is statistically significant," that's statistics. When someone says a model is "overfitting," they're using concepts that live in this part.

This part covers exactly what STA 296 (Intro Statistics) teaches, in the same order it was taught — from "what even is data?" all the way to two-sample hypothesis tests comparing two groups. By the end, you'll have the mathematical reasoning layer that makes all the machine learning you've already learned click into place.
